Set expectations at pre-assessment: what the day will feel like, the analgesia plan, recovery milestones and the discharge criteria the patient must meet. Optimise anaemia, glycaemic control, blood pressure, smoking and alcohol, and prehabilitate where the wait allows.
Avoid prolonged fasting — clear fluids up to 2 hours before arrival, with carbohydrate loading where used locally.

Pre-emptive paracetamol and a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, local infiltration or a peripheral nerve block for every feasible case, and adjuncts (dexamethasone, lidocaine infusion, ketamine, dexmedetomidine, gabapentinoid in selected patients) instead of routine long-acting opioids.
Warn the patient about block regression and to take oral analgesia before rebound pain begins.

Score PONV risk (Apfel) and give at least two agents to high-risk patients — dexamethasone at induction plus ondansetron at the end, with total intravenous anaesthesia and avoidance of nitrous oxide for the highest risk.

Surgical antibiotic prophylaxis within 60 minutes of incision where indicated, and VTE risk assessment for every patient with mechanical prophylaxis, early mobilisation, and pharmacological prophylaxis where risk is high.

Neither dry nor flooded: about 1–2 L of balanced crystalloid for most day cases reduces PONV, dizziness and fatigue, whereas excess fluid delays discharge through bladder distension and oedema. Encourage oral intake as soon as the patient is awake — drinking is part of the pathway, not merely a discharge criterion.
Early mobility and short-acting anaesthesia

Propofol, remifentanil or fentanyl, sevoflurane or desflurane, and quantitatively confirmed reversal of neuromuscular blockade so the patient is awake, clear-headed and able to sit and walk within the hour.
Fast-track suitable patients from theatre directly to phase 2 recovery, then to a chair, oral fluids and mobilisation.

Track day-case rates against BADS procedure-specific targets, unplanned admission rate (aim below 2%), readmission and return-to-theatre rates, pain and PONV scores in recovery and at 24 hours, and patient-reported experience and quality of recovery.
Audit the reason for every overnight admission — pain, PONV, retention, bleeding, a late finish and lack of an escort are all modifiable.
Generic instructions are frequently described as too little, too general, or given at the wrong moment.

Deliver key information at pre-assessment when the patient can absorb it, repeat it at discharge with the escort present, and adapt it to the individual — their procedure, analgesia, job, caring responsibilities and language. Written or digital material supplements a conversation; it does not replace one.

Patients struggle to distinguish normal recovery from complications: they under-report pain, mistake block regression for something going wrong, worry about bruising and swelling, and delay seeking help so as not to be a nuisance.

Give concrete descriptions of what is expected and for how long, alongside unambiguous red flags — pain uncontrolled by the prescribed analgesia, persistent vomiting, inability to pass urine, fever, spreading wound redness or discharge, calf pain or breathlessness, and heavy bleeding.
Continuous professional and personal support

A named 24-hour contact number, a next-day follow-up call and a clear route back into the service reduce anxiety and avoidable emergency attendances. Involve the escort or carer directly in the discharge conversation, because they give the analgesia and decide when to seek help.
Identify patients without support before the day of surgery rather than in recovery.
Recovery does not follow a fixed timetable. Fatigue, disturbed sleep, low mood, dizziness and poor appetite are common for several days and often take patients by surprise.

Give realistic procedure-specific advice on returning to work, driving, exercise, lifting and sexual activity, and on the 24-hour restrictions after anaesthesia, and encourage patients to arrange help at home rather than assuming they will be back to normal the next day.
Use patient-reported outcome and experience measures — quality-of-recovery scores, pain and PONV at 24 hours, satisfaction with information — and feed the results back into the pathway.
Recurring themes such as unrelieved pain on the first night, unexpected retention or confusion about analgesia timing usually indicate a fixable process rather than a difficult patient.
Fasting: 6 h food, 4 h breast milk, 2 h clear fluids — with active encouragement to drink clear fluids up to 2 h before arrival rather than prolonged starvation.

Which medicines to take on the morning of surgery (antihypertensives, inhalers, analgesics) and which to omit (some diabetes drugs, DOACs, GLP-1 agonists per local policy). Bring regular medicines, inhalers and CPAP device.
Leave valuables and jewellery at home, wear loose clothing, arrange childcare and time off work, and expect the whole day in the unit even for a short procedure.
Consent for the possibility of admission

Discuss and document that 1–3% of day cases require unplanned overnight admission — for pain, PONV, urinary retention, bleeding, extended surgery or unexpected findings — so that admission is a planned contingency rather than a perceived failure.

Given to both patient and escort, in plain language: wound and dressing care, analgesic ladder with doses and timings, when to expect the block to wear off and to take analgesia before rebound pain, expected recovery milestones, and activity restrictions (no driving, operating machinery, alcohol, or signing legal documents for 24 h; longer if opioids continue).

A named 24-hour telephone contact for the unit or on-call team, and explicit red flags prompting contact: uncontrolled pain, persistent vomiting, inability to pass urine, fever, increasing wound redness or discharge, calf pain or breathlessness, and heavy bleeding.

Reduce every drug by about 50% and lengthen the interval between increments to allow for prolonged arm–brain time — propofol 10–20 mg increments, midazolam 0.5 mg increments, fentanyl 12.5–25 µg.

Expect exaggerated hypotension from blunted baroreflexes and diastolic dysfunction, and a high risk of delirium and prolonged recovery. Avoid benzodiazepines where possible; prefer a low-dose single agent plus generous local anaesthesia.

STOP-BANG ≥5 or known OSA: sit the patient up (30–45° ramped), pre-oxygenate, use nasal high-flow or CPAP-supported sedation, and capnography throughout. Avoid opioid–benzodiazepine combinations, which produce supra-additive apnoea. Titrate to lean/ideal body weight for boluses.
Have the difficult-airway trolley and a plan for rescue ventilation immediately available, and extend recovery monitoring with continuous SpO₂.
In severe aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, pulmonary hypertension or poor ventricular function, small doses of propofol can cause an irreversible fall in coronary perfusion.

Prefer midazolam/remifentanil or remimazolam over propofol, run a vasopressor drawn up (phenylephrine 50–100 µg, metaraminol 0.25–0.5 mg), consider invasive arterial monitoring, maintain sinus rhythm and preload, and treat hypotension immediately rather than waiting.

Severe COPD, restrictive disease or home oxygen: hypercapnic drive means opioids and benzodiazepines cause CO₂ narcosis before desaturation. Use minimal opioid, capnography (accepting a raised baseline EtCO₂), controlled oxygen rather than high FiO₂, and sit the patient up.
Have naloxone and flumazenil, and non-invasive ventilation, available.

Cirrhosis reduces clearance and increases free drug fraction (hypoalbuminaemia) — midazolam accumulates markedly and may precipitate encephalopathy; remifentanil and remimazolam are the safest choices because metabolism is organ-independent.
In renal failure, avoid morphine and pethidine (active metabolites) and reduce midazolam (active glucuronide accumulates).
Chronic opioid, benzodiazepine, gabapentinoid or alcohol use produces both tolerance (higher dose requirement) and cross-synergy (sudden apnoea).

Continue baseline opioid, use a titrated multimodal approach with ketamine or regional/local supplementation, avoid competing partial agonists, and never assume a “standard” dose is safe. Active stimulant intoxication is a reason to defer.
Sedation should follow national paediatric standards with age-appropriate dosing, two-person practice and a practitioner competent in paediatric airway rescue.

Children desaturate quickly and readily pass from moderate to deep sedation; intranasal dexmedetomidine or midazolam and ketamine are commonly used, with propofol reserved for anaesthetists. Neonates and infants under 1 year, and children with OSA or syndromic airways, should be managed by anaesthetists.
Aspiration risk from about the second trimester, difficult airway, and fetal drug exposure.

Non-urgent sedation should be deferred; where necessary, use aspiration prophylaxis, left lateral tilt after 20 weeks, minimal short-acting drug doses, avoid prolonged benzodiazepine exposure, and involve obstetric anaesthesia with fetal monitoring as indicated.
Urgent procedural sedation (reduction, cardioversion, drainage) is often unfasted.

Weigh the aspiration risk against delay, use the lowest effective depth, keep suction and tipping capability immediately to hand, and consider ketamine (relative airway-reflex preservation) or conversion to a rapid sequence induction in theatre if deep sedation is required.

How Often Transfers Go Wrong, and What Reduces the Risk

AAGBI 2009 grades the patient, not the transfer: critical-care dependency Levels 0–3. Level 2 and 3 patients (organ support, advanced respiratory support) must be escorted by competent, trained and experienced personnel — usually a doctor and a nurse or paramedic.

Three timed phases of transport ventilation: (1) brief bag-valve hand-ventilation while moving between machines, (2) switch to a turbine-driven transport ventilator that replicates ICU settings (mode, TV, PEEP, FiO₂) — observe ≥15 min before departure with continuous ETCO₂, and (3) O₂ cylinder/FiO₂ planning plus disconnection prevention.

The checklists and staffing rules on this page come from studies of how often, and how, things go wrong during transfers. This lesson sets out the numbers and how strong the evidence behind each preventive measure is.
The decision to transfer is made consultant-to-consultant; a consultant is not required to travel on every transfer. Staffing, monitoring and vehicle choice escalate with dependency.

>Normal gap does not mean normal acid–base balance

In the simplified normal-gap model, a bicarbonate fall is accompanied by a chloride rise, keeping the sum of measured anions, and therefore AG, approximately unchanged.

>What is actually being compared?

The commonly named osmolar gap compares measured serum osmolality, preferably by freezing-point depression, with an estimate from sodium, urea and glucose. Osmolality is per kilogram of water; osmolarity is per litre of solution.

>Three independent variables within a chemical model

The Stewart model applies electroneutrality, mass conservation and dissociation equilibria. Its independent variables are PaCO₂, strong ion difference (SID) and total non-volatile weak acids (Atot, principally albumin and phosphate).

>Circuit anticoagulation is not systemic calcium control

Pre-filter citrate binds ionised calcium to inhibit circuit coagulation. Some calcium–citrate complex leaves in the effluent; the remainder returns to the patient. Calcium replacement compensates for losses.

>Acidosis is a process; acidaemia is a pH finding

High anion gap metabolic acidosis means a metabolic acidifying process accompanied by excess unmeasured anions. A low pH is common but not essential: concurrent respiratory or metabolic alkalosis can leave the pH normal or raised.

>Who BICAR-ICU studied

BICAR-ICU enrolled adults within 48 hours of ICU admission with severe metabolic acidaemia: pH 7.20 or lower, PaCO₂ 45 mmHg or lower and bicarbonate 20 mmol/L or lower, plus a SOFA score of 4 or more or lactate of 2 mmol/L or more.

>Chemistry is settled; outcome is not

In Stewart terms, 0.9% sodium chloride contains equal sodium and chloride, so large volumes lower plasma strong ion difference and produce a hyperchloraemic, normal anion gap acidosis. That is a predictable effect on the blood gas.

Why clinically important alkalaemia matters
Alkalosis is a process; alkalaemia is the measured state

Establish pH, PaCO₂ and bicarbonate, then assess whether the respiratory response fits the metabolic process. Hypoventilation can compensate for metabolic alkalosis, but lung disease, respiratory muscle dysfunction and controlled ventilation can limit that response.

>Vomiting and gastric drainage: acid and chloride loss generate the disorder, while volume contraction and potassium depletion can maintain it. Quantify ongoing losses and consider why drainage remains necessary.

DKA involves substantial water and sodium depletion. Initial resuscitation uses crystalloid boluses guided by blood pressure, perfusion and comorbidity, followed by a structured replacement schedule with regular reassessment.

In this subgroup analysis of the SMART and SALT-ED cluster-randomised trials, adults with DKA randomised to balanced crystalloids reached resolution faster than those given saline (median 13.0 vs 16.9 hours).

Total-body potassium is depleted in DKA even when the measured value is normal or high, because acidosis and insulin deficiency shift potassium out of cells. Insulin and fluid both drive it back in, so the measured value falls during treatment.

The two definitions are close but not identical — the consensus accepts bicarbonate at or above 18 mmol/L as an alternative to pH, while JBDS tells you not to use bicarbonate. This page adopts the JBDS wording for UK practice; know that exam questions and overseas protocols may use the consensus version.

SGLT2 inhibitors promote urinary glucose loss and can precipitate euglycaemic DKA during fasting, surgery or acute illness. The CPOC/JBDS 2023 perioperative guideline advises stopping dapagliflozin, empagliflozin and canagliflozin 3 days before surgery and ertugliflozin 4 days before.

Neither bicarbonate nor phosphate replacement is routine in DKA. Bicarbonate has not shown outcome benefit in trials and carries risks (paradoxical CSF acidosis, hypokalaemia); consider it only in life-threatening acidosis with senior input.

Cerebral oedema is the feared complication — predominantly in children and young adults; treat deterioration in conscious level during treatment as an emergency with senior review. This escalation framing is teaching synthesis; thresholds follow local policy.

Capillary or venous blood beta-hydroxybutyrate is the preferred measurement: urine dipsticks detect acetoacetate, lag behind the blood picture and can paradoxically appear to worsen as treatment converts beta-hydroxybutyrate to acetoacetate. This page adopts the 2016 Japan Thyroid Association / Japan Endocrine Society (JTA/JES) thyroid storm guideline as its main framework, because it is openly readable and gives graded recommendations; the 2016 American Thyroid Association (ATA) guideline is quoted where the two differ.
Hormone levels overlap with uncomplicated thyrotoxicosis, so organ dysfunction defines storm
Step 1 — stop new hormone synthesis

JTA/JES favours short-acting beta-1-selective drugs (landiolol, esmolol, or oral bisoprolol). Propranolol is the traditional choice in many UK and US texts because it also modestly reduces T4-to-T3 conversion, but JTA/JES does not recommend it for tachycardia in storm.

the main anaesthetic lesson is prevention. Elective surgery in an uncontrolled thyrotoxic patient should be postponed until they are clinically euthyroid. For urgent surgery, prepare with an antithyroid drug, beta-blockade, steroids and (after the antithyroid drug) iodide, with endocrine input.
Quotations are the sources' own wording; the surrounding explanation is teaching synthesis.

Normal IAP in the critically ill ≈ 5–7 mmHg. IAH = sustained IAP ≥ 12 mmHg. ACS = sustained IAP ≥ 20 mmHg WITH new organ dysfunction (WSACS 2013).
the medical options are suggestions, so use them as a time-limited trial while reassessing. Overt ACS with new organ dysfunction is the recommended indication for decompression.
Grades: I 12–15, II 16–20, III 21–25, IV > 25 mmHg. Grade alone does not define ACS — new organ dysfunction is required.
Fluid is a modifiable cause:
after initial resuscitation, aim to avoid an ongoing positive balance. Removing fluid with diuretics or RRT may be reasonable in an individual patient, but WSACS made no recommendation for them.

Primary ACS = intra-abdominal/pelvic pathology (trauma, ruptured AAA, pancreatitis, peritonitis). Secondary ACS = extra-abdominal cause, typically massive resuscitation (burns, sepsis). Recurrent ACS = re-develops after decompression.

No. WSACS 2013 could make no recommendation about APP monitoring. It is a reasonable physiological concept, but not an evidence-based target.
Abdominal perfusion pressure (APP = MAP − IAP) appears in the ACS definition (with or without APP < 60 mmHg), but WSACS 2013 made NO recommendation on using APP to guide resuscitation.

WSACS medical bundle (5 domains): (1) evacuate intraluminal contents (NG, rectal tube, prokinetics); (2) evacuate intra-abdominal collections (percutaneous drain); (3) improve abdominal-wall compliance (analgesia/sedation, brief NMB trials, body position, escharotomy); (4) optimise fluid administration (avoid a positive balance after resuscitation — WSACS made no recommendation on diuretics, albumin or RRT); (5) optimise systemic and regional perfusion.
Most are weak suggestions on low-quality evidence.

Surgical decompression: indicated for ACS unresponsive to medical management. Midline laparotomy left open with temporary abdominal closure; WSACS recommends negative-pressure wound therapy and protocolised efforts to achieve early, or at least same-hospital-stay, fascial closure.
WSACS recommends measuring IAP whenever any risk factor is present: e.g.

abdominal surgery, major trauma or burns, prone position, ileus, pancreatitis, intra-abdominal fluid or infection, damage-control laparotomy, massive fluid resuscitation or positive balance, acidosis, hypothermia, mechanical ventilation, PEEP > 10, obesity, sepsis, shock.

Prognosis: IAH developing during the ICU stay independently predicted mortality (RR 1.85) in a multicentre mixed ICU cohort; admission IAP did not. WSACS rated the overall evidence base as generally low quality.

Injury or disease in the abdominopelvic region that frequently needs early surgical or radiological intervention — abdominal trauma (haematoma, packing), ruptured AAA, severe pancreatitis, perforated viscus / peritonitis, mesenteric ischaemia, ileus, post-laparotomy haemorrhage, retroperitoneal bleed.

No intra-abdominal injury — typically massive resuscitation: major burns > 30 % TBSA, septic shock, prolonged CPR, polytrauma without abdominal injury, capillary-leak states. WSACS defines it simply as IAH/ACS from conditions that do not originate in the abdominopelvic region.
Recurrence after surgical or medical resolution of a previous episode — usually in patients with an open abdomen who fail to achieve early fascial closure or develop ongoing capillary leak.
WSACS 2013 risk factors — measure IAP if any are present (frequency per local protocol)

> Diminished abdominal-wall compliance (abdominal surgery, major trauma, major burns, prone positioning) · Increased intraluminal contents (gastroparesis/distension, ileus, colonic pseudo-obstruction, volvulus) · Increased intra-abdominal contents (pancreatitis, haemo-/pneumoperitoneum or fluid collections, infection/abscess, tumour, excessive laparoscopic insufflation, cirrhosis with ascites, peritoneal dialysis) · Capillary leak / fluid resuscitation (acidosis, damage-control laparotomy, hypothermia, high APACHE II/SOFA, massive resuscitation or positive balance, polytransfusion) · Others (age, bacteraemia, coagulopathy, raised head-of-bed angle, massive incisional hernia repair, mechanical ventilation, obesity, PEEP > 10, peritonitis, pneumonia, sepsis, shock)<InlineRef topicId=
>Pathophysiology — a multi-organ disease
Pathophysiology — a multi-organ disease
> Raised IAP transmits to every adjacent compartment and impairs venous return globally.
> Polycompartment syndrome describes raised pressure in two or more anatomical compartments simultaneously.

Raised IAP is transmitted through the diaphragm to raise intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and raises central venous pressure; this in turn raises intracranial pressure and worsens cerebral perfusion. The abdominal, thoracic, cranial and limb compartments interact — a rise in one compartment
Polycompartment syndrome

describes raised pressure in two or more anatomical compartments simultaneously. Raised IAP is transmitted through the diaphragm to raise intrathoracic pressure, which reduces venous return and raises central venous pressure; this in turn raises intracranial pressure and worsens cerebral perfusion.
The abdominal, thoracic, cranial and limb compartments interact — a rise in one compartment's pressure, and abdominal-wall compliance itself, influences the others
↓ IVC return → ↓ preload, ↓ CO; ↑ intrathoracic pressure → falsely elevated CVP/PAOP; ↑ SVR and PVR.
Diaphragmatic splinting → ↓ FRC and chest-wall compliance → ↑ plateau and peak pressures, hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, V/Q mismatch. Mimics ARDS.
Renal vein compression + ↓ cardiac output + ↑ renal parenchymal pressure → oliguria → AKI. Oliguria is common and may not respond to fluid challenge.
↑ intrathoracic pressure obstructs cerebral venous drainage → ↑ ICP, ↓ CPP. Particularly dangerous in TBI.
↓ mesenteric perfusion → mucosal ischaemia, bacterial translocation, lactic acidosis, anastomotic breakdown. Hepatic congestion → impaired lactate clearance and drug metabolism.
Ischaemia of rectus sheath → necrosis, dehiscence, surgical-site infection, late ventral hernia.

What is the difference between innate and adaptive immunity?
Innate immunity is the rapid (minutes to hours), non-specific first line — physical barriers, complement, neutrophils, macrophages, NK cells and pattern-recognition receptors. It has no memory.

Adaptive immunity is slower to start (days), highly specific through T-cell receptors and B-cell immunoglobulins, and forms long-lived memory. The two arms are linked by dendritic cells, which sample pathogens and present antigen on MHC to prime naïve T cells.

> When are ancillary tests indicated? Only when the clinical determination cannot be completed or is unreliable — an unexaminable cranial nerve or limb (severe facial/ocular trauma, high cervical cord injury), an apnoea test that cannot be safely performed or must be abandoned (refractory hypoxaemia, haemodynamic instability, ECMO, pre-existing CO₂ retention), or a confounder that cannot be reversed or excluded within a reasonable time.

Only when the clinical determination cannot be completed or is unreliable — an unexaminable cranial nerve or limb (severe facial/ocular trauma, high cervical cord injury), an apnoea test that cannot be safely performed or must be abandoned (refractory hypoxaemia, haemodynamic instability, ECMO, pre-existing CO₂ retention), or a confounder that cannot be reversed or excluded within a reasonable time.
Ancillary tests do not replace clinical testing and are never used to overrule it; they establish the
absence of intracranial blood flow
CT angiography
— the pragmatic first-line test in most UK and European centres. Principle: intracranial pressure exceeding arterial pressure abolishes cerebral perfusion, so intracranial vessels fail to opacify. A
4-point scoring system

is applied 60 s after contrast: absent opacification of the cortical segments of both middle cerebral arteries (M4) and both internal cerebral veins scores 4/4 and confirms circulatory arrest, with the superficial temporal arteries used as an internal control for adequate contrast delivery.
False positives (apparent flow) occur with decompressive craniectomy or an open fontanelle, where ICP cannot rise sufficiently.
Four-vessel catheter angiography

— the historical international gold standard, demonstrating no filling at the level of the carotid bifurcation and circle of Willis. Now largely superseded because it is invasive, requires transfer to the angiography suite and a large contrast load, and offers no diagnostic advantage over CTA.
Radionuclide perfusion imaging / SPECT

— technetium-99m HMPAO scintigraphy showing the "empty skull" sign (absent cerebral uptake with preserved scalp activity). Unaffected by sedative drugs and metabolic derangement, and can be performed portably, which makes it useful where drug confounding cannot be excluded; availability out of hours is the limitation.
EEG and somatosensory evoked potentials
— tests of

, not flow, and therefore limited: EEG is suppressed by sedatives, hypothermia and metabolic derangement (exactly the confounders prompting the test), records only cortical activity and not the brainstem, and is vulnerable to ICU electrical artefact.

What are the four domains of ANTS (Anaesthetists

An operational debrief is an after-action conversation about how the team worked: what happened, what helped, what obstructed care and what should change next time. It is not a retrospective test of the most junior clinician, a substitute for incident investigation, or a treatment for traumatic stress.

Speaking up in a crisis means making a safety concern audible, understandable and actionable, then checking that it has been addressed. Merely thinking that the leader must have noticed is not communication.

>TeamSTEPPS means Team Strategies and Tools to Enhance Performance and Patient Safety. The AHRQ framework organises teachable teamwork behaviours around communication, team leadership, situation monitoring and mutual support, with team structure at the centre.
The Evidence Behind Non-Technical Skills Tools
Task management, team working, situation awareness and decision making — each with behavioural markers used for structured debrief and assessment (Fletcher et al., BJA 2003).
AHRQ TeamSTEPPS describes accurate event reconstruction, analysis, reinforcement of effective behaviours and a method for incorporating lessons into the next plan.

TeamSTEPPS places advocacy and assertion within mutual support: the person raising a concern and the person receiving it both have responsibilities. The purpose is safer shared decision making, not winning an argument.

ENT & Head and Neck

Removal of the entire larynx, usually for cancer, permanently separates the trachea from the pharynx. The trachea is sutured to the neck skin as an end stoma; the pharynx is closed for swallowing. Neck dissection or flap reconstruction may be added.
Partial laryngectomy preserves different anatomy and is not covered by this sequence.
Supine, head supported with agreed neck extension; protect irradiated or restricted cervical tissues and maintain access to the airway and lines.
Review endoscopy/imaging, tumour obstruction, prior radiotherapy, nutrition and the resection/reconstruction plan; agree primary and rescue airway strategies.

Stridor, a friable tumour or restricted neck/mouth opening can make induction hazardous. An awake approach or awake surgical airway may be appropriate after specialist assessment; avoid assuming a standard asleep oral intubation will be safe.
Establish anaesthesia and the agreed airway; expose the neck and perform neck dissection if indicated.

Secure the tube away from the field and keep rescue access available. Assess access/arterial monitoring and blood availability by anticipated extent; previous radiotherapy increases technical difficulty.
Mobilise the larynx, divide the trachea and transfer ventilation to a sterile cuffed tube through the distal trachea.

Explicitly coordinate the airway handover. Protect the cuff from cutting instruments; use airway-fire precautions around an open oxygenated trachea. Confirm sustained waveform capnography, depth and fixation before abandoning the previous airway.
Remove the larynx, close or reconstruct the pharyngeal defect, and mature the permanent tracheal end stoma; a voice prosthesis may be placed.

After separation, mouth/nose oxygen and oral intubation cannot reach the lungs. Check stomal-tube depth to avoid endobronchial placement; flap reconstruction adds prolonged surgery, perfusion and donor-site considerations.
Complete haemostasis, drains and airway checks; transfer with a laryngectomy-specific handover and bedhead sign.

Oxygenation, suction and any ventilation are through the stoma. Ensure humidification, suitable emergency equipment and trained staff. Monitor bleeding, plugging and swelling; do not remove a TEP voice prosthesis during routine airway troubleshooting.
Induction with a potentially obstructed tumour airway
Tracheal division and transfer of ventilation
Permanent loss of mouth-to-lung connection
Postoperative stoma obstruction or bleeding
A total laryngectomy is not a tracheostomy: the upper airway no longer connects to the lungs. If anatomy is uncertain in an emergency, oxygenate face and stoma until clarified.
Plan multimodal analgesia, nutrition, communication support and postoperative care with the head-and-neck team. Pharyngocutaneous fistula and wound problems are later surgical concerns.
These are typical high-level stages, not a dissection guide; combined neck dissection/flap work changes duration and blood-loss risk. Emergency recommendations follow NTSP.
Resection of part or all of the tongue for cancer. A small accessible defect may be closed directly; larger defects can need regional or free-flap reconstruction, sometimes with neck dissection.
The extent and location of resection determine airway, swallowing and speech consequences; total tongue resection is not equivalent to a small partial glossectomy.
Supine with head supported; oral access and tube route agreed before draping. A flap donor site may need simultaneous access and careful limb positioning.
Review tumour site/extent, mouth opening, endoscopy/imaging, bleeding, swallowing, aspiration risk, nutrition and prior radiotherapy.

Agree the primary airway and rescue plan with the surgeon. Large tongue/base-of-tongue lesions can obstruct ventilation and be damaged by instrumentation; consider awake airway management in an at-risk patient.
Secure the airway using the agreed route and expose the oral cavity; elective tracheostomy may be performed for extensive surgery.
Nasal intubation can improve oral access when appropriate, but is not mandatory or suitable for every case. Plan postoperative airway protection before resection, not after swelling appears.
Resect the involved tongue with oncological margins; control lingual vessels and perform neck dissection if indicated.

Bleeding can be brisk and enter the shared airway. Track suction losses and haemoglobin by clinical need; recheck the tube after retractors or head movements. Margins and resection extent are surgical decisions.
Close the defect or reconstruct with a flap; free-flap vessels are joined to recipient neck vessels and perfusion assessed.

Maintain temperature, oxygenation and adequate perfusion without indiscriminate fluid loading. Goal-directed fluids and judicious vasopressors may be appropriate; protect donor-site pressure points and communicate perfusion concerns.
Check haemostasis and the reconstructed airway; recover with planned tracheostomy care, delayed extubation or selected immediate extubation.

Tongue/floor-of-mouth oedema, flap bulk and haematoma can obstruct the airway and make reintubation difficult. Extubation requires an assessed rescue plan and appropriate monitoring; no single strategy suits all resections.
Initial airway control with a friable or obstructing tumour
Lingual vessel bleeding in a shared airway
Flap reperfusion and prolonged reconstruction
Postoperative obstruction from oedema, flap bulk or haematoma

Tracheostomy is not routine for every small partial glossectomy, but may be essential for extensive or high-risk resections; evidence from selected reconstruction cohorts cannot override individual assessment.
Plan opioid-sparing analgesia, aspiration precautions, enteral nutrition and speech/swallow rehabilitation with the multidisciplinary team.
Blood loss and care requirements rise with neck dissection, extensive resection and free-flap reconstruction; the moderate-risk badge is qualitative, not a predicted volume.

A rigid suspension laryngoscope exposes the larynx for magnified inspection, biopsy or treatment of vocal-fold lesions. Cold instruments or a laser may be used. The surgeon and anaesthetist share the same narrow airway; stenosis or an obstructing lesion can make a short procedure high risk.
Supine in an individually suitable laryngoscopy position; protect teeth, lips, eyes and cervical spine. Suspension limits airway access.
Review airway symptoms, endoscopy, lesion/stenosis, respiratory reserve and cervical/dental issues; agree surgical and ventilation plans.

Stridor and severe obstruction demand specialist planning, including rescue access and whether spontaneous breathing should initially be preserved. Select a small tube or a specialist tubeless technique according to lesion, access and team expertise.
Induce anaesthesia using the agreed approach and establish ventilation; protect teeth and insert the suspension laryngoscope.

Insertion is strongly stimulating. TIVA is often useful for open-airway techniques; muscle relaxation depends on the strategy. Reassess ventilation and tube/catheter position after suspension rather than assuming the airway is unchanged.
Inspect the larynx under magnification and perform biopsy or the planned lesion treatment.

A small tracheal tube may restrict surgical access and increase resistance. Tubeless approaches need explicit oxygenation, ventilation and rescue plans; oxygen insufflation alone does not guarantee carbon-dioxide clearance.
If jet ventilation or laser treatment is selected, apply its dedicated safety plan throughout treatment.
Jet ventilation requires unobstructed expiration: impaired egress can cause gas trapping and barotrauma. Monitor oxygenation and CO2 by methods appropriate to the technique.

For laser use, choose wavelength-appropriate laser-resistant equipment when a tube is used, minimise oxidiser enrichment as safely feasible, avoid nitrous oxide and coordinate ignition/oxygen delivery. Tubeless oxygen also carries fire risk.
Secure haemostasis, remove instruments and reassess the airway before emergence and recovery.

Look for bleeding, oedema or residual obstruction; suction appropriately and agree extubation or continued airway support. Watch for laryngospasm, stridor, hypoventilation and barotrauma; recovery/discharge depends on airway status, not just procedure length.
Induction with laryngeal obstruction
Suspension — restricted access or displaced tube
Jet ventilation — inadequate expiration and barotrauma
Laser activation — airway fire
Emergence — laryngospasm or oedema
Small-tube ventilation, intermittent apnoea, spontaneous ventilation and jet ventilation are alternatives with different limitations; none is a default for all lesions.
Jet pressures, frequencies and apnoea intervals require specialist equipment and patient-specific protocols, not values inferred from this summary.

For suspected airway fire, stop surgery and oxidiser delivery, remove burning airway material and extinguish with saline/water, then re-establish ventilation and assess injury according to the local emergency protocol.
Paediatric
Removal of diseased teeth, sometimes alongside restorations, during one general anaesthetic. The dental team and anaesthetist share the airway; the extent of treatment is agreed before starting.
Supine with head supported; dental access, tube route and table rotation agreed with the team.
Review the dental plan, consent, medical history, fasting and airway; agree recovery and discharge arrangements.
Assess age, respiratory illness, obstructive sleep apnoea and comorbidities. Complex or high-risk children need an appropriate paediatric service, not simply a longer routine day-case slot.
Induce anaesthesia and secure an airway compatible with the dental work; nasal tracheal intubation is common when suitable.
The airway is shared and may become inaccessible. Confirm tube position, fixation and the rescue plan; nasal instrumentation can itself cause bleeding.
Examine the teeth; extract the planned teeth, with local anaesthetic and restorative treatment where indicated.
Record all local anaesthetic administered by both teams to avoid cumulative toxicity. Suction blood and debris; communicate before moving the head or applying instruments near the tube.
Achieve socket haemostasis and clear the mouth; confirm removal of any throat pack used.
A throat pack is not automatically required. If used, its insertion and removal must be explicitly recorded and checked; do not rely on a pack to replace airway protection or suction.
Recover the airway and observe until appropriate for discharge.
Anticipate laryngospasm, obstruction, pain, nausea and bleeding. Choose the extubation strategy by aspiration and airway risk; give carers clear bleeding, hydration and analgesia advice.
Airway instrumentation and restricted access
Blood/debris during extraction
Pack-removal check if used
Emergence — laryngospasm or obstruction
Blood loss is usually small but must be judged against the child's size and extent of surgery.
Coordinate multimodal analgesia and antiemetics without duplicating drugs given by the dental team.
Service guidance supports the care setting; it does not prescribe the extraction technique.

Removal of the foreskin for an agreed indication. This entry concerns hospital surgery in children, not neonatal bedside device circumcision; technique and anaesthesia depend on age and clinical circumstances.
Supine, with warming and modesty maintained; local access without excessive leg abduction.
Confirm indication, consent and operative plan, including anatomical abnormalities and bleeding history.
Assess age, prematurity, respiratory illness and day-case suitability; postoperative respiratory observation is individualised.
Provide anaesthesia and analgesia: commonly general anaesthesia with a penile/ring block or another agreed regional technique.
Selected infants may have spinal anaesthesia in experienced services. Track total local anaesthetic across all injections; a block does not remove the need for respiratory monitoring.
Prepare the field, release adhesions as required and excise the foreskin using the planned technique.
Check that analgesia is adequate before incision. Surgical methods vary; this is not a cutting or block-placement guide.
Control bleeding, suture skin edges and apply the planned dressing.
Persistent bleeding warrants surgical reassessment, even when the expected blood loss is low. Avoid assuming a distressed child only has pain.
Recover and provide wound, pain and urinary advice.
Plan opioid-sparing analgesia; review bleeding and ability to pass urine according to the service's discharge pathway. Former preterm infants may need extended observation.
Regional/local injection — cumulative dose
Incision before block onset
Bleeding and postoperative urinary problems
General, local and neuraxial approaches are not interchangeable in every child.
Use age- and risk-appropriate recovery arrangements; no universal discharge time is set here.

Closure of a patent processus vaginalis causing an indirect hernia. Open herniotomy or laparoscopic closure may be used; routine childhood repair usually does not require the mesh reinforcement used in adults.
Supine; open groin exposure or laparoscopic abdominal ports.
Confirm side, reducibility, urgency and evidence of incarceration or compromised bowel.
An incarcerated hernia can bring dehydration, obstruction and aspiration risk; it is not equivalent to a well elective infant. Assess prematurity and respiratory risk.
Induce anaesthesia or establish an agreed regional technique in a selected infant.
An awake spinal approach can reduce some early respiratory events but does not abolish postoperative apnoea risk; sedation and conversion plans matter.
Open approach: expose and separate the sac from cord structures. Laparoscopic approach: inspect the internal ring and hernia contents.
Maintain warmth. Laparoscopic insufflation affects ventilation and venous return; communicate pressure and positioning concerns rather than applying adult assumptions.
Reduce contents and close the sac neck/internal ring while protecting adjacent structures.
If bowel is compromised, the operation and postoperative needs may expand. Contralateral inspection or repair is an individual surgical decision, not automatic.
Close and recover with a risk-based respiratory and analgesia plan.
Former preterm and young infants may need monitored admission. Observe for apnoea irrespective of apparently uncomplicated surgery or the anaesthetic technique.
Incarceration — possible obstruction
Infant induction or regional conversion
Pneumoperitoneum if laparoscopic
Postoperative apnoea risk
Adult hernia guidance and routine mesh repair should not be transferred to infants.
Regional analgesia and local infiltration can reduce opioid requirements; discharge depends on infant risk and local policy.
Cardiothoracic

Repair of native valve leaflets/chordae and often the annulus, or replacement with a prosthesis. Sternotomy and minimally invasive approaches differ; this entry does not cover transcatheter edge-to-edge repair.
Supine for sternotomy; modified supine for right mini-thoracotomy, with peripheral cannulation access if planned.
Review lesion, ventricular and right-heart function, pulmonary pressures and the operative approach; establish monitoring and anaesthesia.
Mitral stenosis and regurgitation have different haemodynamic priorities. Avoid generic valve targets; assess rhythm, filling and cardiac output using the actual lesion and physiology.
Expose the heart, anticoagulate and cannulate for cardiopulmonary bypass; clamp the aorta and give cardioplegia.
Confirm anticoagulation and bypass readiness. Peripheral cannulation adds limb/vascular risks; minimally invasive work may require lung isolation and makes airway access harder.
Open the left atrium and repair or replace the valve.
Coordinate perfusion, temperature and blood conservation. Repair may use a ring and leaflet/chordal techniques; the chosen repair is not represented by one universal sequence.
Close, de-air, release the clamp and separate from bypass with transoesophageal echocardiographic assessment.

Assess residual regurgitation/gradient, ventricular function and complications such as systolic anterior motion after repair. Troubleshoot low output with the surgeon and perfusionist rather than treating every cause alike.
Reverse anticoagulation when agreed, achieve haemostasis and transfer to cardiac critical care.
Plan bleeding surveillance, rhythm/pacing and ventilatory support. Postoperative antithrombotic treatment depends on repair versus prosthesis, rhythm and the cardiology/surgical plan.
Induction in severe valve disease
Cannulation and anticoagulation
De-airing and separation from bypass
Residual valve dysfunction or low output
High bleeding risk reflects bypass and major cardiac surgery, not a predicted transfusion requirement.
TOE use requires expertise and assessment of contraindications; minimally invasive and sternotomy pathways differ.

Removal of an entire lung, usually for malignancy. This is more physiologically demanding than lobectomy; postoperative reserve, right-heart load and protection of the remaining lung dominate planning.
Lateral decubitus with the operative side uppermost; approach may be open or minimally invasive.
Confirm resection extent and cardiopulmonary fitness, including predicted postoperative lung function and exercise assessment when indicated.
Review right ventricular function, pulmonary hypertension and previous treatment; a completion pneumonectomy can be especially complex. Agree analgesia and postoperative care before induction.
Induce anaesthesia, establish lung isolation and position laterally.
Confirm device position bronchoscopically and recheck after positioning. Protect dependent pressure points and ensure access to the airway and vascular lines.
Enter the chest and dissect the hilum, dividing pulmonary vessels and the main bronchus in the surgeon's chosen sequence.
Anticipate major vascular bleeding and hypoxaemia during one-lung ventilation. Communicate before vessel occlusion; protect the ventilated lung and investigate sudden haemodynamic change.
Remove the lung and check bronchial stump closure, haemostasis and the surgical drainage plan.
Stump tests require coordinated ventilation. Drain management after pneumonectomy is procedure-specific; do not automatically apply lobectomy suction practices.
Close, restore two-airway communication as appropriate and recover for close respiratory/cardiac surveillance.
Use careful, individualised fluid management to avoid both hypoperfusion and remaining-lung oedema. Watch for respiratory deterioration, arrhythmias and right-heart dysfunction.
One-lung ventilation — hypoxaemia
Hilar vessel division — major bleeding
Bronchial stump and drainage plan
Remaining-lung injury and postoperative arrhythmia
Avoid fluid overload; a rigid fluid volume is not prescribed by this summary.
Analgesia must allow effective breathing and coughing without excessive sedation. Planned recovery location reflects physiological risk, not operation name alone.
General & GI

A small gastric pouch is joined to a Roux limb of jejunum; a second bowel join reunites it with the biliopancreatic limb. The excluded stomach usually remains in situ. This differs from sleeve gastrectomy and one-anastomosis bypass.
Supine, usually head-up during laparoscopy; secure against sliding and protect pressure points.
Review bariatric assessment, obstructive sleep apnoea, cardiometabolic disease, airway and thromboprophylaxis plans.
Plan preoxygenation, airway equipment and postoperative respiratory support; obesity does not itself justify treating all patients as having identical aspiration or airway risk.
Induce anaesthesia, position and establish laparoscopic ports/pneumoperitoneum.
Rapid desaturation and difficult mask ventilation may occur. Reassess tube position, ventilation and haemodynamics after insufflation and head-up positioning.
Create the small gastric pouch and divide the jejunum to form the Roux and biliopancreatic limbs.
Stapling/dissection can cause bleeding. Coordinate any gastric tube positioning or withdrawal before stapling; prevent accidental incorporation of the tube.
Construct the gastrojejunostomy and jejunojejunostomy, in the surgeon's chosen order; close relevant mesenteric defects.
Maintain stable perfusion and ventilation through a potentially prolonged operation; technique and limb lengths vary and are not prescribed here.
Check the joins as planned, remove instruments and recover through the bariatric pathway.
Use multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia, PONV prevention and risk-based respiratory support. Unexplained tachycardia, pain or deterioration may indicate bleeding or leak and warrants urgent review.
Induction — limited oxygen reserve

Removal of vitreous through small scleral ports, followed by treatment of retinal pathology. Laser, membrane peeling and gas or silicone-oil tamponade may be used; external scleral buckling is a different or additional technique.
Supine with head still under ophthalmic drapes; postoperative posture depends on the repair.
Confirm eye, indication, previous ocular gas and choice of local/regional anaesthesia with monitored care or general anaesthesia.
Assess ability to lie still and tolerate duration/drapes. Check block risks and cardiopulmonary disease; general anaesthesia may be appropriate when cooperation or airway safety is uncertain.
Prepare the eye and insert pars plana ports with an infusion system.
Prevent coughing, movement and straining during intraocular work. Sedation must not compromise ventilation under restricted-access drapes.
Remove vitreous and perform the indicated retinal repair, such as membrane peeling or laser.

Removal of a herniated lumbar disc fragment compressing a nerve root, through open microscopic or minimally invasive access. It is not a spinal fusion; exposure and extent of disc removal vary.
Usually prone on supports that avoid abdominal compression, with eyes and pressure points protected.
Confirm symptoms, baseline neurology, level, imaging and consent; identify urgent deficits or cauda equina features.
Record neurological deficits before anaesthesia. Agree any neuromonitoring, positioning limitations and postoperative neurological review.
Provide anaesthesia and turn prone with a secured airway and coordinated team.
Recheck tube, ventilation, lines, eyes and pressure areas after turning. The abdomen should not be compressed; prone positioning reduces access for airway rescue.
Confirm the level with imaging, expose the operative area and perform limited bony/ligamentous access as required.
Wrong-level prevention is a team check. Monitor haemodynamics and blood loss; an apparently small operation can still cause a vascular or dural injury.
Identify/protect the nerve root and remove the compressing fragment under magnification.
Communicate unexpected bleeding or physiological change. A dural tear may change the surgical closure and postoperative mobilisation plan.
Check decompression/haemostasis, close, turn supine and recover.

Check limb movement and symptoms against baseline once assessable. New weakness, worsening pain or bladder dysfunction needs urgent surgical assessment rather than attribution to residual anaesthesia.

Manual separation and removal of a retained placenta after vaginal birth under appropriate anaesthesia. Bleeding and haemodynamic state determine urgency; suspected placenta accreta spectrum requires senior obstetric planning, not forced separation.
Lithotomy in theatre, with safe supports and access for haemorrhage resuscitation.
Assess retention, blood loss, uterine tone and haemodynamic state; escalate and prepare theatre.
Visible bleeding may underestimate total loss. Activate the obstetric haemorrhage pathway when indicated, obtain access and prepare blood products according to the clinical situation.
Establish regional or general anaesthesia appropriate to urgency, circulating volume and any existing epidural.
Neuraxial extension is not automatically safe in major hypovolaemia. General anaesthesia needs an obstetric airway and aspiration-risk plan; communicate the resuscitation priorities.
Support the uterus externally and pass a hand through the cervix to locate the placental separation plane.
Ensure adequate anaesthesia and monitor continuing blood loss; uterine manipulation is painful and may provoke rapid physiological change.
Separate and remove the placenta if a safe plane exists; assess completeness and uterine cavity.
If no plane can be found, stop and seek senior help for possible accreta. Do not force detachment; haemorrhage may escalate and require a different operative strategy.
Treat uterine atony/haemorrhage, give prophylactic antibiotics per the adopted protocol and arrange recovery.
Reassess haemostasis, perfusion, coagulation and analgesia. Uterotonic choice and drug doses follow the local obstetric pathway; continue surveillance for bleeding and infection.

Vascular

Endovascular treatment of selected carotid stenoses with a stent. This is not carotid endarterectomy: plaque remains in place, and patient selection, embolic protection and antiplatelet planning are central.
Supine on a radiolucent table; access may be femoral, radial or a selected direct carotid approach.
Confirm the planned access, antiplatelet preparation and baseline neurological examination; obtain arterial access, commonly under local anaesthesia.
Preserve communication for neurological assessment where feasible. Sedation must not obscure a new deficit or compromise ventilation; establish access to the patient despite the imaging equipment.
Navigate catheters and perform angiography to define the lesion.
Review renal function, contrast exposure and allergy history. Access injury may cause groin or concealed retroperitoneal bleeding despite an apparently low-blood-loss procedure.
Administer procedural heparin before crossing the lesion and establish the chosen embolic protection strategy.
Document heparin and anticoagulation monitoring with the operator. Distal filters and proximal flow reversal are different techniques; protection choice is not universal.
Selective predilatation, self-expanding stent deployment and selective postdilatation.
Carotid sinus stimulation can cause bradycardia, hypotension or asystole. Agree anticholinergic preparation and haemodynamic support before balloon inflation; report neurological change immediately.
Completion angiography, removal of protection devices and access closure.

Reassess neurology, blood pressure and the access site. Persistent haemodynamic depression or new headache, seizure or deficit needs urgent assessment; plan observation and the prescribed antiplatelet course.
Lesion crossing — cerebral embolisation
Balloon inflation — bradycardia and hypotension

CIRSE 2024 provides technical standards of practice, not a substitute for individual treatment selection or local emergency pathways.

Open removal of obstructing plaque at the common femoral artery, sometimes extending into its branches. A patch may widen the repair; additional angioplasty or stenting makes this a hybrid procedure rather than a bypass.
Supine with the operative groin exposed; hybrid cases need imaging access and preparation for additional arterial access.
Confirm the revascularisation plan and expose the femoral artery through a groin incision.
General or spinal anaesthesia is selected by the patient and team. Review cardiovascular, renal and diabetic comorbidity and the antithrombotic plan before choosing a neuraxial technique.
Obtain vascular control and open the narrowed artery.
Agree and document the procedural anticoagulation plan; prepare for bleeding during arterial exposure. This is local arterial control, not an aortic cross-clamp.
Remove plaque from the common femoral artery and any involved branch origins.
Maintain stable physiology, warming and adequate analgesia during the period of interrupted limb flow; the extent and duration depend on the disease.
Close the arteriotomy, using a patch where appropriate; restore and check limb flow.
Communicate before restoration of flow and document the postoperative limb assessment. A cold, painful limb or new deficit requires prompt vascular review.
If planned, treat other stenoses with angioplasty or stenting; then close the groin wound.
Hybrid work adds procedure time, imaging and contrast exposure. Monitor the access site and arrange analgesia and observation appropriate to the patient's vascular risk.
Arterial exposure and anticoagulation — bleeding
Restoration of flow and limb assessment
Hybrid angioplasty — additional access and contrast
The NHS leaflet supports the broad sequence and anaesthetic options; GVG supplies the limb-revascularisation context, not fixed anaesthetic drug or pressure targets.

Urology

Placement of a donor kidney in the recipient's lower abdomen, joining its artery, vein and ureter to the recipient. This entry covers implantation, not donor nephrectomy; native kidneys usually remain in place.
Supine; lower abdominal incision into the chosen iliac fossa, with access to the bladder.
Confirm the graft and recipient plan; induce anaesthesia and prepare the lower abdomen.
Check recent dialysis, potassium, acid-base balance, fluid status and cardiovascular disease. Preserve dialysis access; review aspiration risk and renal handling of drugs.
Expose recipient vessels and prepare the graft in the iliac fossa.
Maintain temperature, perfusion and access for resuscitation. Agree timing of locally prescribed immunosuppression and antimicrobial prophylaxis; infusions may have specific haemodynamic risks.
Join the graft vein and artery to recipient vessels under vascular control; the precise sequence varies.
Know when reperfusion is approaching. Use clinical assessment and, where appropriate, haemodynamic monitoring to guide volume rather than loading every patient to a fixed central venous pressure.
Release vascular control and assess graft perfusion.
Anticipate blood-pressure change and reassess potassium, acid-base status and volume. Maintain perfusion without fluid overload; titrated vasopressors may be needed despite adequate filling.
Join the donor ureter to the bladder, commonly with a temporary ureteric stent; achieve haemostasis and close.

Monitor urine output and postoperative renal biochemistry. Immediate urine production is not guaranteed and its absence alone does not establish graft failure; delayed graft function needs transplant-team assessment.

Renal clearance alters the duration of several drugs. Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and an appropriate reversal plan are important.
The 2024 anaesthesia review supports balanced crystalloids and assessment of fluid responsiveness; no single fluid volume or pressure target is appropriate for every recipient.
Postoperative analgesia and medication choices must account for changing graft function; follow the transplant service's monitoring and immunosuppression pathway.

Reduction of a groin hernia and reinforcement of the defect, commonly with mesh. Open anterior repair, totally extraperitoneal (TEP) and transabdominal preperitoneal (TAPP) repairs are distinct approaches; tissue repair is an alternative in selected circumstances.
Supine; laparoscopic repair may use head-down tilt. Agree unilateral or bilateral repair and the planned approach.
Open: groin incision with local, general or selected regional anaesthesia. Laparoscopic: ports and creation of the operative space, usually under general anaesthesia.
HerniaSurge recommends local anaesthesia for reducible open repair when the team is experienced. This recommendation is not for laparoscopic surgery or strangulated bowel.
Identify the sac and reduce its contents; assess bowel viability if incarcerated or strangulated.
An emergency obstruction is not an uncomplicated day-case hernia: assess aspiration, dehydration and sepsis risks and agree whether bowel resection may be necessary.
Reinforce the defect, usually with mesh in the tissue plane appropriate to the chosen approach.

During laparoscopy, monitor the effect of insufflation on airway pressures, oxygenation and carbon dioxide, and adjust ventilation. During awake open repair, respond to pain with supplementation rather than excessive sedation.
Complete haemostasis; release insufflation if used and close the wounds.
Use multimodal analgesia and nausea prevention to support mobilisation. Recovery and discharge depend on pain, physiology, social circumstances and any complications, not just the small incision.

Laparoscopic removal of the appendix for appendicitis. Perforation, abscess or peritonitis changes the source-control and postoperative plan; this entry describes surgery once that treatment has been selected.
Supine, with table tilt adjusted for exposure and pressure areas protected.
Induce general anaesthesia; establish laparoscopic access and CO₂ insufflation.
Assess aspiration risk, fasting, vomiting, ileus and physiological disturbance individually. Monitor respiratory mechanics and haemodynamics after insufflation.
Inspect the abdomen, identify the appendix and assess perforation or contamination.
Confirm antimicrobial prophylaxis and communicate any sepsis or hypovolaemia. The operative findings determine whether postoperative antibiotics and higher-acuity observation are needed.
Separate and control the mesoappendix, including its vessels.
Maintain stillness and adequate anaesthesia. Bleeding is usually limited but monitor both surgical bleeding and physiological deterioration.
Secure the appendiceal base, divide the appendix and retrieve it, usually in a bag.
Closure may use ligatures, clips or a stapler according to tissue condition and surgeon judgement; there is no universal device for every appendix.
Complete source control and haemostasis, desufflate and close.
Plan analgesia, nausea prevention and postoperative destination. Routine lavage or drains should not be assumed; the adopted guideline and intraoperative findings guide management.

Do not equate appendicectomy with emergency laparotomy: many uncomplicated cases recover rapidly, whereas complicated disease may need prolonged treatment.

Endoscopic access through the nasal passage and sphenoid sinus to remove a pituitary tumour. Hormone excess or deficiency, proximity to the optic apparatus and carotid arteries, and skull-base reconstruction shape the anaesthetic plan.
Supine, head positioned for endoscopic nasal access, commonly elevated; secure the oral tube away from the surgical field.
Assess endocrine status, vision and airway; induce anaesthesia and secure an oral tracheal tube.
Acromegaly, obesity and sleep apnoea may complicate airway management. Agree cortisol replacement with endocrinology; the review notes variable practice, so no universal steroid regimen is implied.
Clear the nasal corridor and pass the endoscope through the sphenoid sinus towards the sella.
Access to the airway is restricted. If a throat pack is used, record insertion and removal explicitly; monitor cardiovascular responses to stimulation and any locally used vasoactive agents.
Access the pituitary region and resect the tumour under endoscopic vision.
Provide stable neuroanaesthesia and absolute stillness. Carotid injury is uncommon but potentially catastrophic; agree a haemorrhage and interventional neuroradiology rescue pathway.
Achieve haemostasis and reconstruct the skull base if needed, repairing a CSF leak with the chosen graft or material.
A thigh or abdominal donor site may need preparation and analgesia. Avoid emergence that disrupts reconstruction; CSF leak management is part of the surgical plan.
Remove any pack, clear blood and secretions and undertake a planned smooth extubation.
Balance avoidance of coughing against an awake, protected airway in higher-risk patients. Check vision and neurology early; monitor sodium, urine output and endocrine function after surgery.

The BJA Education review supports a multidisciplinary endocrine plan, smooth emergence and postoperative neurological assessment; local steroid practices should not be presented as universal guidance.

New polyuria or sodium disturbance needs assessment for arginine vasopressin deficiency (central diabetes insipidus) and other causes. Delayed hyponatraemia may occur after discharge; follow the endocrine monitoring pathway.
Plan postoperative breathing support jointly when sleep apnoea coexists with skull-base reconstruction, rather than assuming nasal positive-pressure treatment is automatically safe.

Manipulation near the carotid sinus can cause sudden bradycardia and hypotension — alert the surgeon (they will usually pause) and treat promptly; have atropine or glycopyrronium ready. Routine prophylactic carotid-sinus blockade is not recommended.

The critical moment for the brain. Maintain blood pressure at or above the patient's baseline to support collateral flow. In an awake patient, test speech, contralateral hand grip and consciousness immediately and repeatedly; under general anaesthesia, cerebral monitoring (e.g.
stump pressure, near-infrared spectroscopy or transcranial Doppler) guides shunt use.

Regional technique: superficial (± intermediate) cervical plexus block with surgical local anaesthetic supplementation; deep cervical plexus block carries more risk (phrenic block, intravascular injection).
Arterial line before induction or block; measure blood pressure in both arms preoperatively and use the higher-reading arm.
Postoperative blood pressure control matters: hypertension raises the risk of hyperperfusion syndrome (headache, seizures, intracerebral haemorrhage) and haematoma.
Cranial nerve injury (hypoglossal, recurrent laryngeal, marginal mandibular) may affect swallowing or the airway after surgery.
Replacement of the aneurysmal infrarenal aorta with a synthetic tube or bifurcated graft through a laparotomy or retroperitoneal approach.

Systemic heparin, then clamping of the iliac arteries and the aorta below the renal arteries.

Cross-clamp raises afterload suddenly: hypertension and possible myocardial ischaemia or LV failure. Anticipate with deeper anaesthesia or vasodilators (e.g. GTN) just before clamping; the higher the clamp, the bigger the effect and the greater the kidney and gut ischaemia.
Opening of the aneurysm sac, removal of thrombus and oversewing of back-bleeding lumbar arteries.

Proximal then distal anastomosis of a tube or bifurcated graft.
Before declamping, assess volume status and cardiac function, correct hypovolaemia, acidosis, calcium and haemoglobin, and prepare titrated vasopressors — rather than giving a routine fluid load.
Sequential release of the clamps, one limb at a time.

Declamping causes hypotension: sudden fall in afterload, reactive hyperaemia and washout of acid, potassium and vasodilators from the ischaemic legs. Agree slow, staged release with the surgeon; give fluid and vasopressors; reclamp if pressure collapses.
Closure of the sac over the graft, retroperitoneum and abdomen; check leg and bowel perfusion.
Watch for colonic ischaemia, lower limb ischaemia (trash foot) and abdominal compartment syndrome after closure.

Plan critical care admission after surgery.
Renal protection: the main strategies are maintaining perfusion pressure and normovolaemia and minimising clamp time; no drug has proven renal protective benefit.
Coronary disease is common in this group; perioperative myocardial injury is a leading cause of death.

NICE NG156 recommends offering open repair (rather than EVAR) for unruptured infrarenal aneurysms unless there are anaesthetic or medical contraindications or a hostile abdomen — EVAR has lower early mortality but more long-term reintervention.
A covered stent graft is passed from the femoral arteries and deployed inside the aneurysm to exclude it from the circulation.
Supine on a radiolucent table with arms out of the X-ray field; often in an interventional suite or hybrid theatre.
Femoral artery access — open cut-down or percutaneous puncture with closure devices.
Can be done under general, regional or local anaesthesia with sedation; the patient must lie flat and still for a long time.
Heparin, then guidewires and sheaths passed into the aorta; angiography to mark the renal arteries.
Iodinated contrast: protect the kidneys with adequate hydration and avoid nephrotoxins. Breath-holding on request improves imaging.
Deployment of the main body of the stent graft just below the renal arteries.

Cannulation of the contralateral gate and deployment of the iliac limb(s).

Hypothermia is less of a problem than with open repair but procedures can be long.
Emergency control of haemorrhage from a ruptured aneurysm, by open repair or emergency EVAR when anatomy allows.
