Bleeding from uterine vessels can be brisk; ureteric injury is a surgical risk near this step.
Colpotomy (cutting the vagina around the cervix) and removal of the uterus vaginally.
Loss of pneumoperitoneum is common at this point.
Closure of the vaginal vault and port sites.
High PONV risk: multimodal prophylaxis. Check for facial and airway oedema after long head-down.
Steep head-down with pneumoperitoneum
Uterine vessel division
Emergence — PONV
ERAS gynaecological/oncology guidance supports minimal fasting, carbohydrate loading, PONV prophylaxis, opioid-sparing analgesia and thromboprophylaxis.
Lithotomy carries risk of common peroneal nerve injury and compartment syndrome in long cases.
Breast & Plastics
Removal of breast tissue (with sentinel node biopsy or axillary clearance) and same-operation reconstruction with an implant or the patient's own tissue, such as a free DIEP flap from the abdomen.
Supine with arms out on boards; sat up during surgery to check symmetry.
Mastectomy and axillary surgery; blue dye or isotope may be used for sentinel node.
Blue dye can cause falsely low pulse oximetry readings and, rarely, anaphylaxis.
Implant reconstruction: pocket formed and implant placed. Flap reconstruction: abdominal flap raised on deep inferior epigastric vessels.
Regional options include paravertebral or chest wall fascial plane blocks; for flaps, abdominal wall (e.g. TAP or rectus sheath) catheters help.
Free flap: microvascular anastomosis to the internal mammary vessels.
As for any free flap: warm, well filled but not overloaded, adequate blood pressure; avoid prolonged vasoconstriction.
Patient sat up to check shape; closure with drains.
Secure the airway and lines before sitting up; check blood pressure after position change.
Blue dye injection
Flap anastomosis
Sitting the patient up
ERAS breast reconstruction consensus supports PONV prophylaxis, multimodal analgesia, normothermia and avoiding fluid excess.
Chronic post-mastectomy pain is common; good acute analgesia may help.
Day-case removal of the clouded lens by ultrasound and insertion of an intraocular lens, usually under local anaesthesia.
Supine and flat, head still, face draped; the patient must be able to lie flat for the procedure.
Local anaesthesia: topical with intracameral, sub-Tenon's, or less often peribulbar/retrobulbar block.

Needle blocks carry risks of globe perforation, retrobulbar haemorrhage and brainstem anaesthesia; sub-Tenon's and topical reduce needle risk. Monitoring, IV access and resuscitation equipment must be available.
Small corneal incisions; capsulorhexis (opening the lens capsule).
The patient must stay still and avoid coughing; check they can lie flat and communicate. Minimal or no sedation is preferred.
Phacoemulsification of the lens and aspiration.
Ocular manipulation can trigger the oculocardiac reflex (bradycardia), though less often than in squint surgery.
Intraocular lens inserted; incisions self-seal.
Patient goes home the same day.
Needle block placement
Patient movement during intraocular steps
Over-sedation under drapes with no airway access

Joint RCoA/RCOphth guidance: routine fasting is not required for topical or sub-Tenon's LA without sedation, and routine blood tests are not needed; check anticoagulation but usually continue it (block choice may change).
General anaesthesia is reserved for patients who cannot cooperate or lie still.
Division of the hypertrophied pyloric muscle down to the mucosa in an infant with hypertrophic pyloric stenosis. A medical, not surgical, emergency: fluid and electrolyte correction comes first.
Supine infant on a warmed table; open right upper quadrant/umbilical incision or laparoscopic ports.
Preoperative resuscitation and correction of the hypochloraemic, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis.
Do not list the infant until electrolytes and acid-base status are corrected per local paediatric criteria; alkalosis is associated with delayed emergence and postoperative apnoea.
Gastric emptying before induction via nasogastric or orogastric tube (gastric ultrasound may be used to assess the antrum).
Aspiration risk is high. Ensure adequate depth and complete neuromuscular block before laryngoscopy; agree the induction technique (rapid sequence or modified) with the team.
Access to the pylorus (open or laparoscopic) and delivery of the pyloric 'olive'.
Laparoscopic insufflation in an infant reduces compliance and can raise end-tidal CO₂; keep the infant warm.
Longitudinal seromuscular incision and splitting of the muscle until the mucosa bulges; mucosal integrity may be tested with air via the gastric tube.
The surgeon may ask for air to be injected down the gastric tube to check for a leak — be ready.
Closure and local anaesthetic infiltration or block.
Analgesia options include rectus sheath block, TAP block or wound infiltration; minimise opioids and extubate fully awake. Monitor for apnoea postoperatively.
Induction — regurgitation and aspiration
Mucosal perforation check
Emergence and early postoperative period — apnoea
Surgery is never an emergency before metabolic correction.
Regional or local techniques reduce opioid need in this apnoea-prone age group.
Exact laboratory targets and induction technique are local-pathway decisions; this summary does not set them.

One or two burr holes are made over a chronic subdural collection, the membrane is opened, the liquefied haematoma is irrigated out and a drain is usually left. Patients are often elderly and anticoagulated.
Supine with the head turned and supported on a head ring; head-up tilt per surgeon.
Preoperative review: neurology, anticoagulant/antiplatelet use and reversal plan, comorbidities.
Agree reversal with the neurosurgical and haematology teams. Older patients with frailty and cardiac disease are common.
Anaesthesia: general anaesthesia or local anaesthesia with or without sedation, depending on patient and surgeon.
General anaesthesia allows ventilatory control; local techniques avoid airway instrumentation but require a cooperative, still patient. Avoid hypercapnia and hypotension.
Scalp incision and burr hole(s); dura and outer membrane opened.
Scalp infiltration helps analgesia; the release of a large collection may cause transient haemodynamic change.
Irrigation of the cavity with warm saline; drain placement (subdural or subperiosteal).
Surgeons may request a Valsalva manoeuvre to help expel fluid and air — coordinate with ventilation.
Closure; postoperative drain management and neurological observation.
Plan a smooth emergence with prompt neurological assessment; prevent PONV and screen for delirium.
Anticoagulation reversal before incision
Membrane opening and decompression
Emergence — neurological reassessment
Choice of anaesthesia depends on neurological status, haematoma size and location and surgical approach.
Recurrence is common; reoperation patients need the same review.
Local-versus-general comparisons are largely observational; do not treat them as proof of superiority.
Arthroscopic repair or decompression in the shoulder through several small portals with fluid distension of the joint. Pain can be severe; position carries haemodynamic and cerebral risks.
Beach chair (sitting) or lateral decubitus with arm traction.
Regional anaesthesia: interscalene brachial plexus block or a phrenic-sparing alternative (e.g. suprascapular plus axillary nerve blocks).
Interscalene block causes ipsilateral phrenic nerve palsy in most patients — caution in respiratory disease. Consider alternatives; check for Horner's, hoarseness and local anaesthetic toxicity.
Positioning in beach chair or lateral; head secured in neutral.
In beach chair, cerebral perfusion pressure is lower than arm BP suggests; correct BP measurement for height difference and avoid hypotension. Protect eyes, neck and pressure points.
Portal placement and joint distension with irrigation fluid; surgeon may request controlled hypotension for visibility.
Agree acceptable BP limits — deliberate hypotension in the sitting position risks cerebral ischaemia. Fluid can extravasate into neck tissues; check airway at the end.
Repair (anchors, sutures) or decompression; closure of portals.
Awake or sedated surgery under block is possible; otherwise GA with a secured airway accessible despite drapes.
Block placement — phrenic, vascular and neuraxial complications
Sitting up — hypotension and cerebral hypoperfusion
Rebound pain when the block wears off
Integrate preoperative education, regional anaesthesia and multimodal postoperative analgesia.
Plan for rebound pain on block regression with regular oral analgesia.
Oral & Maxillofacial

Fracture fragments are reduced, the teeth placed in correct occlusion, and the bone fixed with miniplates through intraoral (or sometimes external) incisions. The surgeon needs the teeth to meet, which shapes airway choice.
Supine, head ring, shared airway with the surgeon; table often turned 90–180°.
Airway assessment: mouth opening (trismus from pain versus mechanical block), bleeding, associated head, cervical spine and midface injuries.
Plan the airway jointly. Options include videolaryngoscopy, awake tracheal intubation, nasal intubation, submental intubation or tracheostomy, depending on injuries and occlusion needs.
Intubation — commonly nasotracheal, so the teeth can be brought together.
Nasal intubation is avoided or approached cautiously if there are midface or skull-base fractures. Secure the tube well; throat pack per local safety checks.
Intermaxillary fixation (temporary or arch bars) to restore occlusion.
Once jaws are fixed, there is no oral access to the airway. Know how and who removes the fixation.
Fracture reduction and miniplate fixation through intraoral incisions; fixation released if not required postoperatively.
Ensure haemostasis and remove the throat pack before emergence; suction the pharynx.
Extubation fully awake, with postoperative airway plan.
If the jaws stay wired, wire cutters must accompany the patient and staff must know how to use them. Give antiemetics to reduce vomiting with fixed jaws.
Induction and intubation
Intermaxillary fixation — loss of oral airway access
Throat pack removal and extubation
Facial trauma may coexist with brain and cervical spine injury.
Senior anaesthetic input and teamwork are required; direct laryngoscopy may not be the safest option.

Staged reconstruction of the lip (typically in infancy) and palate (later in infancy) by a cleft team. The airway is shared with the surgeon, can be difficult, and is at risk of obstruction after palate repair.
Supine with head ring and shoulder roll (neck extended); table turned; patient fully draped.
Preoperative assessment for associated syndromes and congenital anomalies, feeding, weight and recent respiratory infection.
Cleft anomalies are associated with numerous congenital abnormalities; look specifically for features predicting difficult laryngoscopy and for cardiac disease.
Induction and oral intubation with a preformed south-facing RAE tube secured in the midline below the lower lip.
Laryngoscopy may be difficult (blade can fall into the cleft); confirm tube tip position visually and by auscultation, since the preformed curve may not fit the child.
Positioning with neck extension; throat pack; for palate surgery, insertion of the Dingman mouth gag.
Recheck the tube after every move. The gag can kink or displace the tube or raise airway pressures, and throat pack insertion/removal can cause accidental extubation.
Infiltration with local anaesthetic and adrenaline; lip or palate repair.
Infiltration reduces bleeding and adds analgesia. Use multimodal analgesia and titrate opioids carefully because of the risk of respiratory events.
Throat pack removal, suction under direct vision and awake extubation; postoperative airway monitoring.
Oropharyngeal/nasopharyngeal swelling in nasal-breathing infants can obstruct the airway; a nasopharyngeal airway or tongue suture may be placed. Monitor for obstruction throughout recovery.
Laryngoscopy and intubation
Mouth gag insertion and head movement — tube kinking or displacement
Extubation and recovery — airway obstruction
Effective communication with the surgeon about the shared airway is essential.
Timing of lip and palate surgery and analgesic doses follow the local cleft team protocol; this summary does not set them.

An opening is made in the anterior trachea (usually around the second to fourth rings) and a tracheostomy tube inserted, for prolonged ventilation, airway obstruction or head and neck surgery. The most dangerous moment is the handover from the tracheal tube to the tracheostomy tube.
Supine with shoulder roll and neck extended (if the cervical spine allows); head ring.
Planning: indication, airway plan if the tracheostomy fails, anticoagulation, and equipment (tube sizes, capnography).
Agree in advance who withdraws the tracheal tube and when; have a plan for re-intubation from above.
Neck incision, division of strap muscles and division or retraction of the thyroid isthmus.
Bleeding from the isthmus or anterior jugular veins is possible. Keep the patient deeply anaesthetised and paralysed.
Opening of the trachea (window or flap).
Reduce inspired oxygen as far as is safe and stop diathermy before the trachea is opened — airway fire risk. The cuff may be punctured if the tube is not withdrawn appropriately.
Withdrawal of the tracheal tube under direct vision until its tip is just above the stoma, then insertion of the tracheostomy tube.
Do not remove the tracheal tube fully until correct tracheostomy placement is confirmed by sustained capnography; then remove it.
Securing the tube (ties/sutures), chest auscultation and handover with bedhead signs.
Displacement in the early days is dangerous because the tract is not formed; follow National Tracheostomy Safety Project emergency algorithms.
Tracheal opening — airway fire and cuff damage
Tube exchange — loss of the airway
Early displacement after surgery
Confirm placement with waveform capnography every time.
Ensure the ward knows whether the upper airway is patent (tracheostomy) or not (laryngectomy).

Removal of the kidney with its fat and fascia, usually for renal cell carcinoma. Most cases are laparoscopic or robotic; tumour extending into the renal vein or inferior vena cava (IVC) turns it into a major open vascular operation.
Lateral (flank) with the table broken, or supine for open transperitoneal and IVC cases.
Preoperative staging including the level of any venous tumour thrombus; assessment of renal function and the remaining kidney.

Thrombus level dictates the plan: higher levels may need large-bore access, cell salvage discussion, transoesophageal echo and, rarely, cardiopulmonary bypass. Plan for reduced renal reserve afterwards.
Positioning in the lateral flank position with kidney rest and table break.
Lateral flexion can reduce venous return and cause hypotension; protect the dependent arm, eyes and brachial plexus, and check ventilation of the dependent lung.
Mobilisation of the kidney; control and division of the renal artery, then the renal vein.
Sudden bleeding from the renal vessels or IVC is the main intraoperative danger. Pneumothorax can follow pleural breach in flank approaches.
For IVC thrombus: clamping of the IVC above and below the thrombus, cavotomy and thrombus removal.
Caval clamping can sharply reduce venous return and cardiac output; the thrombus can embolise to the lungs — echo helps track it. Coordinate clamping with the surgeon.
Haemostasis and closure; postoperative analgesia and renal monitoring.
Epidural, wound catheters or multimodal analgesia depending on approach; avoid nephrotoxins and dose renally cleared drugs for the new renal function.
Renal hilum and IVC dissection — massive bleeding
Caval clamping — loss of venous return
Thrombus manipulation — tumour embolism
Most uncomplicated nephrectomies are low-to-moderate blood loss; IVC extension changes this fundamentally.
High-level thrombus cases belong in high-volume multidisciplinary centres.

Craniotomy during which the patient is awake for part of the operation, so speech or movement can be tested while the surgeon maps and removes tumour near eloquent cortex. Communication, comfort and airway access are central.
Supine or semi-lateral, head in pins; drapes arranged so the patient's face can be seen and the airway reached.
Patient selection and preparation: ability to cooperate, anxiety, airway, obesity and sleep apnoea; rehearsal of intraoperative tests.
Poor cooperation and difficult airway are relative contraindications; agree the technique (sedation/monitored care or asleep-awake-asleep) with the team.
Scalp block and pin-site infiltration; head fixation.
Effective local anaesthesia is essential whatever technique is used; respect maximum local anaesthetic doses.
Bone flap and dural opening under sedation or general anaesthesia (supraglottic airway in asleep-awake-asleep).
Avoid hypercapnia and airway obstruction with sedation; dural opening is painful unless infiltrated.
Awake phase: cortical stimulation mapping and tumour resection while the patient talks or moves.
Patient must be awake but comfortable. Seizures can be provoked by stimulation — have cold saline for the cortex and anticonvulsant drugs ready. Watch for nausea, pain and agitation.
Closure, often with sedation or general anaesthesia resumed; early neurological assessment.
Plan smooth emergence or deepening; continue PONV prophylaxis and pain control.
Airway obstruction or apnoea during sedation
Intraoperative seizure during stimulation
Loss of cooperation in the awake phase
No single technique is optimal; choose for the patient and surgeon.
A supraglottic airway, or conversion to general anaesthesia, must be immediately available.

Pedicle screws and rods are used to straighten and fuse a curved spine, usually in adolescents. Neuromuscular scoliosis (cerebral palsy, muscular dystrophies) carries much higher respiratory, cardiac and bleeding risk than idiopathic scoliosis.
Prone on a spinal frame with abdomen free; head in a pressure-relieving headrest.
Preoperative assessment: lung function, cardiac function (especially muscular dystrophies), nutrition, seizures and secretions; postoperative critical care bed.

Neuromuscular patients have a higher risk of perioperative complications; plan for postoperative ventilation or non-invasive support where reserve is poor. Avoid suxamethonium in muscular dystrophies.
Induction, large-bore access, arterial line; prone positioning.
Protect eyes, face, breasts/genitals and limbs; keep the abdomen free to lower venous pressure and bleeding.
Exposure and pedicle screw insertion across many levels.
Blood loss can be large: tranexamic acid and cell salvage are commonly used. Total intravenous anaesthesia suits motor evoked potential monitoring; avoid neuromuscular block after baseline.
Rod insertion and curve correction.

Highest risk of spinal cord injury. If neuromonitoring signals fall, raise blood pressure, correct anaemia and temperature, and agree with the surgeon whether to release correction or do a wake-up test.
Bone graft, closure and postoperative care.
Multimodal analgesia (often intrathecal morphine or PCA); monitor for respiratory depression, ileus and ongoing bleeding.
Correction manoeuvre — spinal cord ischaemia
Major blood loss during long instrumentation
Blood pressure, haemoglobin and anaesthetic depth all affect neuromonitoring — keep them stable.
Exact transfusion and tranexamic acid regimens follow local protocols; this summary does not set them.

The diseased liver is removed and a donor liver implanted, with vascular anastomoses (caval, portal, arterial) and biliary reconstruction. Three phases — dissection, anhepatic and neohepatic — each bring distinct anaesthetic problems, peaking at graft reperfusion.
Supine with arms out; access for large-bore lines, cell salvage and possible venovenous bypass.
Assessment of end-stage liver disease: coagulopathy, portopulmonary hypertension, hepatopulmonary syndrome, hepatorenal syndrome, cardiomyopathy and sarcopenia.
Portopulmonary hypertension and cardiac disease can make transplant unsafe; check echocardiography and right heart assessment per the transplant unit protocol.
Dissection (pre-anhepatic) phase: mobilisation of the native liver despite portal hypertension and collaterals.
Major bleeding is common: large-bore access, rapid infuser, cell salvage and point-of-care viscoelastic testing guide replacement. Monitor for hypocalcaemia from citrate.
Anhepatic phase: vascular clamping (caval or piggyback technique) and removal of the native liver.
Venous return falls with full caval clamping; no liver means no citrate or lactate clearance and worsening acidosis. Watch potassium.
Graft implantation and reperfusion through the portal vein.

Post-reperfusion syndrome: sudden hypotension, bradycardia, hyperkalaemia and pulmonary hypertension; intracardiac thrombus can occur. Prepare vasopressors, calcium and treatment for hyperkalaemia; transoesophageal echo helps.
Neohepatic phase: arterial and biliary anastomoses, haemostasis; transfer to critical care.
Graft function shows as falling lactate, improving coagulation and acid-base. Avoid fluid overload that congests the graft.
Dissection — massive haemorrhage
Reperfusion — post-reperfusion syndrome and hyperkalaemia
Specialist transplant anaesthesia team; protocols for transfusion and coagulation management are centre-specific.
Intracardiac thrombus and right heart failure may need advanced support including mechanical circulatory support.

Removal of a catecholamine-secreting adrenal tumour, usually laparoscopically. Tumour handling can cause severe hypertension and arrhythmias; after the adrenal vein is tied, blood pressure and glucose can fall sharply.
Lateral decubitus (transperitoneal) or prone (retroperitoneoscopic).
Preoperative preparation with an endocrinologist: biochemical confirmation, cardiac assessment and medical preparation (commonly α-blockade, then β-blockade if needed).
Practice varies: a 21-centre review found many patients had surgery without α-blockade with low complication rates, so follow the local multidisciplinary pathway.
Induction and arterial line before induction; vasodilators and short-acting β-blocker ready.
Avoid triggers of catecholamine release: light anaesthesia, hypoxia, hypercapnia, histamine-releasing drugs and metoclopramide.
Pneumoperitoneum and tumour mobilisation.
Insufflation and handling cause hypertensive surges and tachyarrhythmias; treat promptly (e.g. magnesium, phentolamine, nitroprusside or GTN, esmolol per local practice) and tell the surgeon.
Ligation of the adrenal vein.
Catecholamine levels fall: expect hypotension needing fluid and vasopressors. Stop vasodilators in advance.
Tumour removal, closure and postoperative monitoring in HDU.
Monitor for persistent hypotension and rebound hypoglycaemia; give steroid cover after bilateral adrenalectomy.
Tumour handling — hypertensive crisis
Adrenal vein ligation — sudden hypotension
Early postoperative — hypoglycaemia
Close surgeon–anaesthetist communication during handling is essential.
There are no randomised trials comparing preparation strategies.

Endoscopic clearance of diseased sinus tissue and polyps to restore drainage. Small amounts of bleeding ruin the endoscopic view, so the anaesthetic aim is a still patient and a dry surgical field. The orbit and skull base lie close by.
Supine, reverse Trendelenburg (head-up), head slightly turned towards the surgeon; table often turned.
Preoperative assessment: asthma, aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease, anticoagulants and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Nasal polyps often coexist with asthma and NSAID sensitivity — check before giving NSAIDs.
Topical vasoconstrictor to the nose; induction and airway (reinforced tracheal tube or reinforced supraglottic airway with throat pack).
Topical vasoconstrictors (e.g. cocaine or adrenaline preparations) can cause hypertension and arrhythmias.
Optimising the field: head-up tilt, controlled heart rate and blood pressure.
Evidence favours TIVA over volatile anaesthesia for a better surgical field with less blood loss; tranexamic acid is also used. Agree acceptable blood pressure limits.
Endoscopic uncinectomy, ethmoidectomy and opening of sinus ostia.
Orbital or skull-base injury can occur: watch for sudden eye swelling or CSF leak and tell the surgeon.
Haemostasis, packing, throat pack removal and smooth emergence.
Suction the pharynx under direct vision; avoid coughing and straining. Patients with nasal packs breathe through the mouth.
Topical vasoconstrictor — hypertension and arrhythmia
Bleeding obscuring the field
Orbital or skull-base injury
Very low blood pressure targets risk organ hypoperfusion; balance field quality with patient safety.
Throat pack removal must be part of the sign-out check.

Common traps
Normal: O₂ pulse rises then plateaus at peak exercise

Relying solely on subjective METs (METS study limitation)

Stopping antiplatelet without considering coronary stent timing

Delaying surgery in symptomatic AAA pending optimisation
Minute ventilation (VE) increases progressively during exercise. The ventilatory reserve (MVV − VE peak) assesses whether breathing capacity limits exercise.
Use objective risk stratification (RCRI, NT-proBNP, CPET) and shared decision-making rather than subjective METs alone; pre-habilitate and plan critical care.
Breathing reserve = MVV − VE peak (normal >20% or >11 L/min)

Premedication
Ventilatory equivalents measure how much ventilation is needed per unit of gas exchange. VE/VCO₂ is the most clinically important — it reflects ventilatory efficiency and dead space.

V-Slope (VCO₂ vs VO₂)

An AT <11 mL/kg/min predicts increased postoperative cardiopulmonary morbidity and 30/90-day mortality after major non-cardiac surgery; 11–14 mL/kg/min is intermediate risk and >14 mL/kg/min low risk (Older 1993; POM-HR).

The V-slope plot is the primary method for determining the anaerobic threshold (AT). Below the AT, VCO₂ rises in a 1:1 ratio with VO₂. Above AT, the slope steepens as excess CO₂ is produced from bicarbonate buffering of lactic acid.
When should elective non-cardiac surgery be deferred after PCI?

Elective non-cardiac surgery should be delayed at least 1 month after PCI regardless of stent type. Beyond this, whether to continue or interrupt dual antiplatelet therapy is a multidisciplinary (heart team) decision balancing individual thrombotic risk against surgical bleeding risk (ESC Non-Cardiac Surgery 2022).
AT = inflection point where VCO₂/VO₂ slope changes from ~1.0 to >1.0
How is the Revised Cardiac Risk Index (Lee) interpreted?

Six predictors (high-risk surgery, IHD, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine >170 µmol/L): 0 ≈ 0.4%, 1 ≈ 1%, 2 ≈ 2.4%, ≥3 ≈ 5.4% risk of a major cardiac event at 30 days.
AT <11 ml/kg/min = high perioperative risk for major surgery
Preoperative Assessment
AT 11–14 ml/kg/min = intermediate risk; >14 ml/kg/min = low risk

Very low AT (<8 ml/kg/min): severe cardiac limitation or profound deconditioning. Indeterminate AT may occur with hyperventilation or erratic breathing pattern.
Apply NICE NG45 to choose evidence-based preoperative investigations by ASA × surgical severity
PETO₂ & PETCO₂ vs Time
Manage chronic medications perioperatively (ACE-I/ARB, β-blockers, anticoagulants, GLP-1 RAs, insulin)
End-tidal O₂ (PETO₂) and end-tidal CO₂ (PETCO₂) reflect gas exchange efficiency. PETCO₂ normally rises slightly during exercise (↑ perfusion) then falls above AT as hyperventilation begins.
Diagnose and treat preoperative anaemia using NICE/CPOC PBM pathway with oral vs IV iron
Apply AAGBI/BHS 2016 principles to perioperative blood-pressure management without inappropriate cancellation
At AT: PETCO₂ starts to fall and PETO₂ starts to rise (isocapnic buffering ends)
CPET: AT <11 ml/kg/min or VO₂ peak <15 ml/kg/min = high perioperative risk
Low PETCO₂ throughout = hyperventilation or ↑ dead space
Failure of PETCO₂ to rise in early exercise suggests high dead space (pulmonary vascular disease). Persistently low PETCO₂ with high VE/VCO₂ = poor prognosis in heart failure.
Omit ACE-I/ARBs on day of surgery; continue beta-blockers (POISE: don't initiate perioperatively)

Omit ACE-I/ARBs on day of surgery; continue beta-blockers (POISE: don
Tidal volume (VT) rises with increasing ventilation until it plateaus, after which further increases in VE are achieved by increasing respiratory rate. The pattern reveals ventilatory mechanics.
Functional capacity >4 METs (climb 2 flights) suggests adequate cardiac reserve
Normal: VT rises to ~50–60% of VC then plateaus
Previous difficult intubation is the strongest predictor of future difficulty — always check records
Further VE increase achieved by ↑ respiratory rate
Helps distinguish obstructive from restrictive patterns
GLP-1 RA: hold weekly semaglutide 7 days pre-op; if not held, treat as full stomach (ASA 2023)

Why is goal-directed fluid therapy preferred over fixed-volume regimens in ERAS?

Stroke-volume optimisation with small balanced crystalloid boluses titrated to dynamic indices reduces postoperative complications and length of stay compared with both liberal and overly restrictive fixed regimens (POM-O, OPTIMISE).

By Hagen–Poiseuille — flow is proportional to the fourth power of internal radius and inversely proportional to length. A short, wide-bore (16G or 14G) cannula delivers far greater flow than a longer central catheter of equivalent gauge.
When is a midline preferred over a PICC?

For peripherally compatible therapies of 1–4 weeks duration (e.g. antibiotics, fluids, non-irritant chemotherapy). Vesicants, parenteral nutrition or hyperosmolar/extreme-pH drugs require a central-tip device such as a PICC or CVC.
What are the key complications of internal jugular CVC insertion?

Carotid puncture, pneumothorax (lower than subclavian but not zero), arrhythmias from wire or catheter contact, air embolism, catheter-related bloodstream infection, and late venous stenosis or thrombosis. Ultrasound guidance is mandatory (NICE TA49).

Maintain sinus rhythm, a normal or slightly low heart rate (60–80), adequate preload and high systemic vascular resistance — use phenylephrine or vasopressin first-line for hypotension, and avoid agents that drop SVR or cause tachycardia.
How should a pacemaker-dependent patient be managed when monopolar diathermy is required?

Reprogramme to an asynchronous mode (DOO/VOO) or apply a clinical magnet, position the diathermy return plate so the current path does not cross the device, use short bipolar bursts where possible, and check the device postoperatively.
What are the anaesthetic principles in pulmonary hypertension?

Avoid hypoxia, hypercarbia, acidosis, hypothermia and high airway pressures — all increase pulmonary vascular resistance. Maintain RV preload and coronary perfusion pressure, use noradrenaline or vasopressin for systemic hypotension, and have inhaled pulmonary vasodilators (NO, iloprost) available.
At what blood pressure should an elective case be cancelled for hypertension?
Per the AAGBI/BHS 2016 joint guideline, proceed if pre-assessment BP is <180 mmHg systolic AND <110 mmHg diastolic.

Above this, refer back to primary care for optimisation rather than treating acutely on the day — there is no evidence that short-term in-hospital lowering reduces perioperative cardiac risk and rapid drops may cause harm.
How should ACE inhibitors and ARBs be managed on the day of surgery?

Both ESC/ESA 2022 and the 2024 ACC/AHA perioperative guideline recommend withholding ACE-I/ARB on the morning of surgery when they are prescribed for hypertension, to reduce intra-operative hypotension. POISE-3 (2023) supports this
approach with a MAP target ≥80 mmHg. Restart within 48 h once the patient is euvolaemic with stable renal function.
How do you manage true hypertensive emergency before urgent surgery?

Use an arterial line and titrate IV antihypertensives (labetalol or esmolol for dissection/phaeochromocytoma surge, GTN for ACS/pulmonary oedema, magnesium + labetalol for eclampsia) to lower MAP by no more than 20–25% in the first hour, then to around 160/100 mmHg over 2–6 h.
Treat reversible precipitants (pain, hypoxia, hypercarbia, raised ICP) first. Truly time-critical surgery should not be delayed for chronic hypertension alone.

Ischaemic heart disease, valvular disease, heart failure, arrhythmias, pulmonary hypertension, and congenital heart disease in adults
> Cardiovascular disease is the leading driver of perioperative morbidity and mortality.

This topic covers the conditions most likely to influence anaesthetic planning — ischaemic heart disease, valvular pathology, heart failure, arrhythmias and devices, pulmonary hypertension, and adult congenital heart disease — with a focus on risk stratification, optimisation, and intra-operative goals.
{/* Perioperative Risk Stratification */}
>Risk Prediction Tools
Risk Prediction Tools
Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI, Lee 1999)

— one point each for: high-risk surgery (intraperitoneal/intrathoracic/suprainguinal vascular), history of IHD, history of heart failure, history of cerebrovascular disease, insulin-dependent diabetes, creatinine >170 µmol/L (2.0 mg/dL).
Risk of major cardiac complication: 0 points ≈0.4%, 1 point ≈1%, 2 points ≈2.4%, ≥3 points ≈5.4%
ACS-NSQIP Surgical Risk Calculator / MICA model

— incorporates ASA grade, functional status, procedure type and comorbidities to give a continuous predicted risk of MI or cardiac arrest; performs better than RCRI at the extremes of risk and is endorsed by ACC/AHA 2014 and 2024 as the preferred first step

ESC/ESA 2022 stepwise pathway: (1) urgency of surgery, (2) active cardiac conditions (unstable angina, decompensated HF, severe arrhythmia, severe valve disease), (3) surgery-specific risk (low <1%, intermediate 1–5%, high >5% 30-day cardiovascular death/MI), (4) functional capacity, (5) further testing only if it will change management
>Functional Capacity & CPET
Functional Capacity & CPET
> <li>Functional capacity expressed in metabolic equivalents (METs): 1 MET = resting O₂ consumption (3.5 mL/kg/min).

Climbing a flight of stairs or walking briskly on the flat ≈4 METs; the inability to achieve 4 METs on self-report (Duke Activity Status Index) is associated with increased perioperative and long-term cardiac risk (METS trial 2018 confirmed self-reported METs poorly predict complications, favouring objective testing)
  • Cardiopulmonary exercise testing (CPET) gives objective, reproducible values: anaerobic threshold (AT) <11 mL/kg/min identifies increased perioperative risk, and AT <11 mL/kg/min combined with myocardial ischaemia on ECG during CPET carries the highest risk
  • Peak VO₂ <15 mL/kg/min (or <15–20 mL/kg/min depending on surgery/procedure) is also used as a threshold for high risk before major surgery (e.g.

lung resection, major intra-abdominal or intrathoracic surgery)
  • Ventilatory equivalent for CO₂ (VE/VCO₂ slope) >34–36 is an additional adverse prognostic marker, particularly relevant in heart failure and pulmonary hypertension
  • CPET use is limited by peripheral vascular disease, musculoskeletal limitation and poor patient effort — use pharmacological or imaging stress tests as an alternative when CPET is not feasible

records.t: Detect and treat preoperative anaemia (including iron-deficiency anaemia) using patient blood management principles.
Apply restrictive transfusion thresholds (NICE NG24) and choose appropriate haemostatic adjuncts including tranexamic acid.
Risk-stratify thrombocytopenic patients and select safe platelet thresholds for surgery and neuraxial blockade.
Recognise neutropenia, plan safe anaesthesia, and manage suspected neutropenic sepsis within one hour.

Preoperative anaemia is independently associated with increased mortality, transfusion and complications — screen ≥6 weeks before elective major surgery and treat iron deficiency first (oral if >6 weeks to surgery, IV if <6 weeks)

CPOC (2023) and NATA (2017) recommend identifying anaemia at the point of listing for major elective surgery, allowing at least 6 weeks for investigation and treatment.
A full blood count, ferritin, transferrin saturation, B12, folate and renal function form the minimum panel; CRP is needed to interpret ferritin in inflammation (functional iron deficiency).
What is the safe platelet count for spinal or epidural anaesthesia?

AAGBI (2013) and BSH (2017) support neuraxial blockade with a platelet count ≥80 ×10⁹/L provided the count is stable and the cause of thrombocytopenia is benign. Counts of 50–80 ×10⁹/L require an explicit risk–benefit assessment; below 50 ×10⁹/L neuraxial techniques are generally avoided.
Never transfuse platelets in HIT, TTP or ITP without specialist advice.
How do you manage a patient presenting for emergency surgery with severe thrombocytopenia of unknown cause?

Discuss with haematology before transfusing. Avoid platelets in TTP/HIT (may worsen thrombosis). For life-threatening bleeding, give platelets to a target of >50 ×10⁹/L (>100 for CNS/eye), correct fibrinogen (>1.5 g/L), and consider TXA 1 g.
Use general rather than neuraxial anaesthesia and minimise invasive lines where possible.
What antibiotic should be given for suspected neutropenic sepsis?

Per NICE neutropenic-sepsis guidance, empirical piperacillin–tazobactam 4.5 g IV (or meropenem if previous resistance / β-lactam allergy with cross-reactivity assessment) within 1 hour of recognition, after blood cultures. Add vancomycin or teicoplanin only for suspected line infection, MRSA risk or severe mucositis.
What HbS target is needed before major surgery in sickle cell disease?
A simple top-up transfusion to Hb ~100 g/L is usually sufficient for most surgery and is as effective as exchange transfusion at preventing perioperative complications.

Exchange transfusion to reduce HbS% to below ~30% is reserved for high-risk surgery (bypass, neurosurgery) or patients with a history of severe crises, and avoids the hyperviscosity risk of simple top-up in patients with an already-high baseline Hb.
When is desmopressin useful in a bleeding disorder and when is it not?

Desmopressin 0.3 microgram/kg IV releases stored factor VIII and von Willebrand factor, making it useful in mild haemophilia A and type 1 von Willebrand disease, as well as uraemic or aspirin-induced platelet dysfunction.
It is ineffective in haemophilia B (no effect on factor IX) and type 3 VWD (no VWF stores to release), and should be used cautiously in type 2B VWD (may worsen thrombocytopenia).
How long should a DOAC be omitted before neuraxial anaesthesia?

Intervals depend on the drug and renal function: apixaban/rivaroxaban/edoxaban are typically omitted for 48 hours before a high bleeding-risk procedure or neuraxial block (longer if CrCl 30–50 mL/min), while dabigatran requires 48–96 hours depending on creatinine clearance and is avoided below CrCl 30 mL/min.
Catheters are removed only once the same interval has elapsed since the last dose, and the next dose is delayed for several hours after removal.
What blood products must be irradiated, and why?
Irradiated cellular blood products prevent transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease from viable donor lymphocytes.

They are mandatory for stem cell transplant recipients, granulocyte transfusions, intrauterine/neonatal exchange transfusion, directed donations from blood relatives, patients treated with purine analogues (fludarabine, cladribine, bendamustine), and Hodgkin lymphoma patients.

Tranexamic Acid: Risks and Safe Use
Seizure risk:

TXA is a competitive antagonist at glycine and GABA-A receptors; risk rises with high dose, cardiac surgery (especially open-chamber/on-pump procedures) and renal impairment where clearance is reduced — dose-reduce in renal failure. New myoclonus or seizure requires drug review and supportive management (

can occur with rapid intravenous bolus — give over at least 10 minutes.

  • Use viscoelastic testing (ROTEM/TEG) to guide component therapy in major bleeding
  • Minimise iatrogenic blood loss (microsampling tubes, judicious phlebotomy)

Recognise and treat hepatic decompensation in the perioperative period — acute-on-chronic liver failure, hepatorenal syndrome, hepatic encephalopathy, and variceal bleeding.
Child-Pugh and MELD both predict perioperative mortality; MELD > 15 or Child-Pugh C → defer elective non-transplant surgery if possible (30-day mortality > 25%).
Cirrhosis produces a hyperdynamic circulation (↑CO, ↓SVR), reduced response to catecholamines and high risk of intraoperative hypotension — invasive monitoring is usually warranted for major surgery.
Coagulation in cirrhosis is 'rebalanced' — INR does not predict bleeding, prophylactic FFP is rarely indicated, and VTE risk persists; use TEG/ROTEM to guide product use.
— INR does not predict bleeding, prophylactic FFP is rarely indicated, and VTE risk persists; use TEG/ROTEM to guide product use.
Cisatracurium (Hofmann degradation) is the neuromuscular blocker of choice; avoid drugs with hepatic clearance such as vecuronium/rocuronium for prolonged cases.
Sevoflurane and desflurane preserve hepatic blood flow and have minimal metabolism; halothane is contraindicated because of immune-mediated halothane hepatitis.
Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS-AKI) is treated with terlipressin (or noradrenaline) plus 20% human albumin; avoid nephrotoxins and aim for MAP ≥ 80 mmHg.

Anaesthesia for elective inguinal hernia repair in Child-Pugh B cirrhosis

A 58-year-old with alcohol-related cirrhosis (Child-Pugh B, MELD 14) presents for elective open inguinal hernia repair. Ascites is controlled on spironolactone; platelets 78 × 10⁹/L, INR 1.6. Plan the perioperative assessment and anaesthetic technique.
>Step-by-step reasoning
Step-by-step reasoning
> <li> Confirm risk stratification — MELD 14 → Mayo postoperative 30-day mortality ~10–15% for open abdominal surgery; discuss benefit/burden with patient and hepatology.

• Preoperative optimisation: treat ascites and electrolyte derangement, screen for varices, correct hyponatraemia < 130 mmol/L slowly, vitamin K 10 mg IV if INR > 1.5, manage encephalopathy with lactulose ± rifaximin.
• Coagulation: do not transfuse FFP on the basis of INR alone — check fibrinogen and a viscoelastic trace if available; platelets < 50 × 10⁹/L only if neuraxial planned or active bleeding.

• Technique: regional anaesthesia (TAP block / ilioinguinal block ± light sedation) is preferable to GA in this patient — avoids airway instrumentation, reduces hepatic insult and opioid burden. If neuraxial is chosen, confirm platelets ≥ 80 × 10⁹/L and INR < 1.5 (or use ROTEM/TEG guidance).

• If GA required: propofol with reduced induction dose (↑ free fraction), fentanyl or remifentanil rather than morphine, cisatracurium, sevoflurane maintenance, lung-protective ventilation, avoid hypotension (target MAP within 20% of baseline).

• Postoperative: HDU monitoring, multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia (paracetamol < 2 g/24 h, avoid NSAIDs), early VTE prophylaxis (mechanical immediately, pharmacological once haemostasis confirmed), daily review for encephalopathy and AKI.

Combine Child-Pugh class (A/B/C) and MELD score — MELD <10 is low risk, 10–15 intermediate, and >15 high (>20 prohibitive for elective surgery). The VOCAL-Penn score outperforms MELD for surgical mortality prediction.

Cirrhotic coagulopathy is a rebalanced state — both pro- and anti-coagulant factors are reduced. FFP raises portal pressure (worsening variceal bleeding risk) and adds volume without correcting the underlying defect; thromboelastography (ROTEM/TEG) guides targeted therapy.

Splanchnic vasoconstrictor (terlipressin or noradrenaline) plus 20% human albumin (1 g/kg on day 1, then 20–40 g/day). Diuretics, large-volume crystalloid and low-dose dopamine all worsen outcome; definitive treatment is liver transplantation.
Hepatic Co-Existing Disease
Provision of anaesthesia for the patient with chronic liver disease undergoing non-hepatic surgery

> Patients with chronic liver disease undergoing non-hepatic surgery are a high-risk population whose mortality is driven less by the operation itself than by the severity of underlying hepatic dysfunction.

This topic covers preoperative risk stratification, the multi-system features of cirrhosis that change every step of the anaesthetic, and the specific perioperative complications — hepatorenal syndrome, encephalopathy, variceal haemorrhage and acute-on-chronic liver failure — that the anaesthetist must anticipate and treat.

Child-Pugh Score

>
  • Five components (1–3 points each): bilirubin, albumin, INR (or PT), ascites, encephalopathy.
  • Class A (5–6) — well-compensated; B (7–9) — significant functional compromise; C (10–15) — decompensated.
  • Approximate 30-day perioperative mortality for major abdominal surgery: A ~10%, B ~30%, C > 70%

(ICA 2015 / EASL 2018) — all must be present: (1) cirrhosis with ascites; (2) AKI by KDIGO/ICA criteria (creatinine rise ≥ 26.5 µmol/L within 48 h, or ≥ 50% above baseline within 7 days); (3) no sustained improvement after ≥ 2 days of diuretic withdrawal and volume expansion with 20% albumin 1 g/kg/day (max 100 g/day); (4) absence of shock; (5) no current/recent nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast); (6) no macroscopic structural kidney injury — proteinuria < 500 mg/day, no microhaematuria (< 50 RBC/HPF), normal renal ultrasound

: a bridge to liver transplantation or to recovery from a reversible precipitant, not a treatment for HRS itself; liver transplantation is the only definitive therapy, with simultaneous liver-kidney transplant considered after prolonged dialysis dependence.

VTE prophylaxis must not be omitted — risk of portal vein and deep vein thrombosis is preserved or increased.

Neurological — Hepatic Encephalopathy

records.t: CKD Staging & Uraemic Effects

This section concerns a patient with an established kidney transplant undergoing another operation. Immediate care after the transplant operation itself is a separate specialist pathway: do not import a urine-for-urine replacement regimen or a transplant-centre pressure target into every non-transplant operation.
Preoperative Assessment & Optimisation
Before surgery: establish the graft and medication baseline
Pharmacology in Renal Impairment

Record usual creatinine and its trend, recent graft problems, immunosuppressant names, formulations, doses and timing, and the transplant team’s contact details. Reconcile the actual prescription with the patient and pharmacist: tacrolimus products are not casually interchangeable.
Intraoperative Management
Document a plan for periods when oral dosing is impossible, rather than allowing “nil by mouth” to omit essential medicines.
Electrolyte & Acid-Base Emergencies
RCSEd Transplant 2022
Perioperative AKI

Protect any functioning dialysis fistula in its actual access limb; do not assume its side matches the graft. Establish the graft’s location when pelvic positioning, retraction or surgery could affect it.
The Renal Transplant Recipient
Assess cardiovascular disease, volume state and drug handling from current function, not from the reassuring label “transplanted”.
Stage chronic kidney disease by eGFR (G1–G5) and albuminuria (A1–A3) and describe the multi-system consequences of uraemia relevant to anaesthesia.
NICE NG148
Optimise the dialysis-dependent or CKD patient before surgery, including dialysis timing, fistula protection and management of anaemia and antihypertensives.
Immunosuppression: continuity with specialist exceptions
Modify anaesthetic drug choice and dosing appropriately for reduced renal clearance, including neuromuscular blockers, opioids and drugs to avoid.
UKCPA advises continuing tacrolimus and mycophenolate for elective and emergency surgery with specialist involvement, and giving the next dose when due in the immediate postoperative period.
Plan intraoperative fluid, monitoring and regional anaesthesia strategies for patients with CKD or on renal replacement therapy.

If oral medication cannot be taken, obtain specialist advice on the alternative drug, dose, route and frequency; IV or sublingual administration is not a milligram-for-milligram conversion to improvise.
Recognise and treat hyperkalaemia and other electrolyte/acid-base emergencies using an exact stepwise drug protocol.
UKCPA Mycophenolate
Apply KDIGO/NICE NG148 criteria to prevent and manage perioperative acute kidney injury, and know the evidence for RRT timing.
Sirolimus is different: wound-healing concerns may require an individualised interruption plan. If stopped, UKCPA advises not restarting until adequate healing after specialist consultation.
Describe the specific perioperative considerations for a patient with a functioning renal transplant.

Steroid supplementation depends on the patient’s steroid exposure and surgical stress; liaise with the transplant team and the site’s steroid guidance rather than giving every recipient the same regimen.

CKD is staged by eGFR (G1 ≥90, G2 60–89, G3a 45–59, G3b 30–44, G4 15–29, G5 <15 mL/min/1.73m² or dialysis) combined with albuminuria category (A1 <3, A2 3–30, A3 >30 mg/mmol) — risk of progression and cardiovascular events rises with both axes.
UKCPA Sirolimus

Uraemia causes platelet dysfunction (abnormal platelet–vessel wall interaction despite normal count/coagulation screen), anaemia (reduced erythropoietin), autonomic neuropathy with labile blood pressure, accelerated atherosclerosis, renal bone disease and delayed gastric emptying — treat as 'full stomach' in advanced uraemia.

>Perfusion, interactions and infection

Avoid untreated hypotension and hypovolaemia, but also avoid fluid overload. Individualise haemodynamic support to the baseline pressure, cardiovascular state and operation.

Renal denervation does not justify claiming that intrinsic renal autoregulation is absent or prescribing a universal MAP of 70–80 mmHg; the cited medication guidance does not establish such a target.<R label=

Elective dialysis patients should undergo haemodialysis the day before surgery (not the same day), aiming for a potassium <5.5 mmol/L and near-dry weight; avoid aggressive ultrafiltration immediately pre-theatre which risks hypovolaemia and hypotension.
Perfusion, interactions and infection
Avoid untreated hypotension and hypovolaemia, but also avoid fluid overload. Individualise haemodynamic support to the baseline pressure, cardiovascular state and operation.

Atracurium and cisatracurium (organ-independent Hofmann elimination/ester hydrolysis) are the neuromuscular blockers of choice in renal failure; avoid morphine (active metabolite morphine-6-glucuronide accumulates) and pethidine (norpethidine accumulation causes seizures) — use fentanyl or dose-reduced oxycodone instead.
Renal denervation does not justify claiming that intrinsic renal autoregulation is absent or prescribing a universal MAP of 70–80 mmHg; the cited medication guidance does not establish such a target.

Suxamethonium raises serum potassium by ~0.5–1.0 mmol/L and is not contraindicated in stable CKD, but should be avoided if pre-existing hyperkalaemia, uraemic neuropathy or recent dialysis-related hyperkalaemia is present.

Calcineurin inhibitors are metabolised through CYP3A4. Macrolides such as clarithromycin/erythromycin and azole antifungals may increase exposure; use alternatives where suitable, or arrange careful trough monitoring and specialist dose advice.
Tacrolimus also brings nephrotoxicity, electrolyte and QT-interaction considerations. Check new medicines before prescribing, not after creatinine rises.

Severe hyperkalaemia is treated with a stepwise protocol: calcium chloride 10 mL 10% (or calcium gluconate 30 mL 10%) IV for cardiac membrane stabilisation, insulin 10 units in 25 g glucose (50 mL 50% or 250 mL 10%) IV, nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg, ± sodium bicarbonate if acidotic, with definitive treatment by dialysis.

Monitor for infection and maintain asepsis. Immunosuppression is not an automatic indication for broader or longer surgical antibiotic prophylaxis: select prophylaxis for the procedure and local policy, with transplant/microbiology input when needed.

KDIGO defines AKI as creatinine rise ≥26.5 μmol/L within 48 h, or ≥1.5× baseline within 7 days, or urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for 6 h; STARRT-AKI showed no survival benefit from accelerated RRT initiation over a watchful-waiting strategy guided by conventional indications.

Avoid NSAIDs with tacrolimus and assess the risk of other nephrotoxic exposure. A solitary functioning graft requires careful protection, but “a single kidney has no functional reserve” is not a valid general physiological rule.

A 74-year-old with CKD G4 presents with a perforated sigmoid diverticulum and requires emergency laparotomy. Potassium is 6.9 mmol/L with peaked T-waves and a widened QRS on the ECG. Outline immediate management before and during induction.
> <li> Continuous cardiac monitoring; treat as a medical emergency in parallel with surgical preparation — do not delay life-saving surgery, but stabilise potassium first if at all possible.

• Cardioprotection: calcium chloride 10 mL 10% IV (or calcium gluconate 30 mL 10% if only peripheral access) over 2–5 minutes, repeated if ECG changes persist after 5 minutes — does not lower potassium but stabilises the myocardium.

• Shift potassium intracellularly: insulin 10 units (Actrapid) in 25 g glucose IV (50 mL 50% glucose or 250 mL 10% glucose) over 15–30 minutes, plus nebulised salbutamol 10–20 mg; monitor capillary glucose for at least 4–6 hours after (risk of delayed hypoglycaemia).

Ankylosing Spondylitis
Connective Tissue Disease
Perioperative Drug Therapy
Spinal Deformity & Myopathy
Airway & Regional Checklist
Describe the multi-system manifestations of rheumatoid arthritis relevant to anaesthesia, including cervical spine, airway, cardiorespiratory and haematological disease.
Assess and manage the cervical spine in rheumatoid arthritis, recognising atlantoaxial and vertical subluxation and planning safe airway instrumentation.
Outline the cardiorespiratory, airway and neuraxial implications of ankylosing spondylitis and connective tissue diseases (systemic sclerosis, SLE, Sjögren, Marfan, Ehlers-Danlos).
Apply current guidance on perioperative management of DMARDs, biologics and JAK inhibitors around elective and emergency surgery.
Plan anaesthesia for patients with spinal deformity and neuromuscular disease, including respiratory assessment and positioning/neuromonitoring considerations.

Anterior atlantoaxial subluxation is present in up to 25% of long-standing rheumatoid arthritis — anterior atlanto-dental interval > 3 mm on flexion lateral cervical spine X-ray indicates instability; manual in-line stabilisation and awake fibreoptic or videolaryngoscopic intubation should be considered.
Cricoarytenoid arthritis causes hoarseness, stridor and reduced glottic aperture — anticipate a smaller tracheal tube and possible postoperative stridor.

Ankylosing spondylitis produces a fixed flexion deformity of the cervicothoracic spine, restrictive ventilatory defect, aortic regurgitation with conduction block, and a spine that fractures easily with minimal trauma — awake intubation and a front-of-neck access plan should be considered even for emergency surgery.

Systemic sclerosis threatens the airway (reduced mouth opening, microstomia), the vasculature (Raynaud phenomenon, difficult IV/arterial access), the gut (oesophageal dysmotility — aspiration risk), the lungs (interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension) and the kidney (scleroderma renal crisis, precipitated by high-dose corticosteroid).

Methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine should be continued perioperatively; biologic agents are withheld for one full dosing interval with surgery timed for the end of that interval; JAK inhibitors (e.g. tofacitinib, baricitinib) are stopped 3 days before surgery because of thrombosis and infection risk.
Chronic corticosteroid use requires perioperative steroid cover according to usual dose and surgical stress, because of HPA-axis suppression.

How should biologic and JAK-inhibitor therapy be managed before elective surgery?

Biologics (e.g. TNF-α inhibitors such as adalimumab/infliximab, IL-6 inhibitors) are withheld for one full dosing interval, with surgery timed for the end of that interval to minimise both infection/wound-healing risk and disease flare.

JAK inhibitors (tofacitinib, baricitinib, upadacitinib) are stopped 3 days before surgery because of thrombosis and infection risk. Methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine and sulfasalazine are continued throughout.
Why is systemic sclerosis a particular anaesthetic challenge?

It affects nearly every system relevant to anaesthesia: microstomia limits mouth opening and airway access; Raynaud phenomenon and skin/vascular fibrosis make peripheral and arterial access difficult (avoid unnecessary cannulation, keep the patient warm); oesophageal dysmotility increases aspiration risk; interstitial lung disease and pulmonary hypertension increase perioperative respiratory and cardiac risk; and scleroderma renal crisis can be precipitated by high-dose corticosteroids and hypotension.

A restrictive ventilatory defect develops as the Cobb angle increases; forced vital capacity (FVC) < 40% predicted is associated with a significant risk of prolonged postoperative ventilation, and FVC < 70% predicted warrants careful preoperative respiratory assessment. Neuromuscular scoliosis (e.g.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy) carries additional risks of cardiomyopathy, malignant hyperthermia susceptibility (avoid suxamethonium and volatile agents in dystrophinopathies) and a blunted cough with bulbar weakness.

A 46-year-old with known achalasia presents for elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy. She reports occasional regurgitation of undigested food and a dilated oesophagus on recent barium swallow. Plan her perioperative aspiration risk management.
>Step-by-step reasoning
Step-by-step reasoning

> <li> Recognise achalasia as a high aspiration-risk condition: failure of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation and loss of peristalsis mean food and secretions can pool in a dilated oesophagus regardless of standard fasting time.

Why is a high-output stoma dangerous before anaesthesia?

Outputs above 1500-2000 mL/day cause depletion of sodium, magnesium and water (the small bowel cannot compensate as the colon would), producing a contracted extracellular volume with secondary hyperaldosteronism and a thirsty, hyponatraemic patient who drinks hypotonic fluid and worsens losses further.

Correct with a glucose-saline oral rehydration solution, loperamide/codeine to slow transit, and IV magnesium/sodium replacement guided by daily electrolytes before elective induction; treat as hypovolaemic even with a normal-looking blood pressure.

>Step-by-step reasoning

Current multisociety guidance recommends continuing buprenorphine perioperatively in most cases rather than routine discontinuation, using multimodal analgesia and titrated full-agonist opioids alongside it; stopping risks relapse and does not reliably improve analgesia.
How do you distinguish serotonin syndrome from neuroleptic malignant syndrome?
Serotonin syndrome has a rapid onset (usually <24 h), hyperreflexia, myoclonus and clonus, and diarrhoea; NMS develops over days, features
rigidity, hyporeflexia and very high CK, and follows dopamine antagonist exposure or dopaminergic withdrawal rather than serotonergic drugs.
Why does bradycardia occur immediately after the ECT stimulus?

The electrical stimulus produces an initial brief parasympathetic discharge (vagal outflow) causing bradycardia or even brief asystole, followed within seconds by a sympathetic surge causing tachycardia and hypertension during the tonic-clonic seizure; anticholinergic pre-treatment (glycopyrrolate) may be used in patients at risk of significant bradyarrhythmia.
Can a patient detained under the Mental Health Act refuse anaesthesia for an unrelated surgical problem?

Yes — detention under the Mental Health Act only authorises treatment for the mental disorder itself. Capacity for other treatment decisions must be separately assessed under the Mental Capacity Act 2005; if the patient has capacity for that specific decision, their refusal must be respected.

Reasonable adjustments are a legal duty under the Equality Act 2010, not a courtesy: extra appointment time, quiet environments, first or last on the list, familiar carers present throughout, and communication in the patient's preferred format.

People with a learning disability die younger than the general population, with a large proportion of deaths judged avoidable; diagnostic overshadowing (attributing new physical symptoms to the disability) is a recurring contributory factor identified by the LeDeR programme.

For autistic patients, plan around sensory sensitivities and predictability: minimise waiting, noise, bright light and unnecessary staff changes, allow familiar objects, and follow the patient's own routines and communication tools wherever possible.

A structured, planned premedication strategy (oral or buccal midazolam, oral clonidine, intranasal or buccal dexmedetomidine, oral ketamine, or inhalational induction with sevoflurane) is safer than an improvised struggle at the point of cannulation — see the premedication section of the preoperative assessment topic for doses.

Restraint or clinical holding in a patient who lacks capacity is lawful only when it is necessary to prevent harm and proportionate in degree and duration to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm; it must be planned, documented and reviewed, never used as a substitute for adjustment and preparation.

Prisoners retain the same rights to consent, confidentiality and dignity as any other patient; custody officers may remain for security but clinical information must not be shared with them beyond what is needed for safety, and restraints should be removed for anaesthesia unless a documented risk assessment states otherwise.

Sedation is the last rung of a ladder, not the first: adjustments, preparation, distraction, topical/local and regional techniques and nitrous oxide come before oral, buccal, intranasal or intramuscular drugs.

Consent in this group is a staged process, not a signature: information in the right format, capacity assessed with every support in place, legal instruments checked, and a documented best-interests meeting when the patient cannot decide.

Postoperative distress in a patient who cannot self-report is pain, delirium or a hidden physical cause until proved otherwise: regular multimodal analgesia, an observational pain tool plus carer knowledge, and a familiar supporter at the bedside are the safety net.

A 24-year-old man with severe learning disability, autism and non-verbal communication needs multiple dental extractions. He becomes highly distressed in clinical environments and previously required six staff to hold him for a blood test. Plan the pathway.
>Step-by-step reasoning
Step-by-step reasoning

>
  • Preassessment away from the day of surgery — meet the patient with his family/paid carers, obtain the hospital passport, identify triggers (noise, touch, waiting), calming strategies, favoured distractions, and how he expresses pain.
• Capacity assessment for the specific decision.

If he lacks capacity, hold a best-interests meeting under the Mental Capacity Act 2005 with family, carers, dentist, anaesthetist and (if no one appropriate to consult) an IMCA; document the decision, the least-restrictive option considered and any planned restraint.

• Bundle the procedures — arrange for bloods, ECG, examination, dental treatment and any deferred investigations (e.g. audiology, cervical screening where relevant) under one anaesthetic to avoid repeated distressing episodes.

• Reasonable adjustments — first on the list, admission direct to a quiet side room or straight to theatre, minimal staff, carers present until asleep and in recovery, lights and monitor alarms reduced, no unnecessary gowning or fasting-time drift.

• Planned premedication rather than improvised force: oral or buccal midazolam, or oral clonidine given at home/on the ward with carer support; intranasal or buccal dexmedetomidine and oral ketamine are alternatives where benzodiazepine premedication has previously failed or caused disinhibition.

• Induction — inhalational sevoflurane induction with the patient in a chair or on a trolley, carer-assisted, is often kinder than pursuing intravenous access; secure the cannula only once anaesthetised.

Common traps
list-disc list-inside space-y-1 text-foreground
Bringing the patient to a busy morning ward and only then discovering he will not tolerate cannulation.
Treating physical restraint as the plan rather than as a documented, proportionate last resort.

Emergency appendicectomy in a serving prisoner

A 31-year-old man is escorted from prison to the emergency department with appendicitis. He arrives handcuffed to a custody officer, with two officers in attendance. Discuss the practical and ethical management of his anaesthesia.

>
  • Clinical equivalence — care must be equivalent to that of any other patient. Prison custody is not a reason to alter analgesic, anaesthetic or critical-care decisions.

• Consent and capacity — the prisoner consents for himself exactly as any adult with capacity does; he may refuse surgery. Neither custody staff nor the prison governor can consent for him or override refusal.
• Confidentiality — history-taking should happen out of officers
Clinical equivalence
— care must be equivalent to that of any other patient. Prison custody is not a reason to alter analgesic, anaesthetic or critical-care decisions.
Consent and capacity
— the prisoner consents for himself exactly as any adult with capacity does; he may refuse surgery. Neither custody staff nor the prison governor can consent for him or override refusal.

— history-taking should happen out of officers' hearing wherever the risk assessment allows; share with escorts only the operational minimum (timings, likely admission, mobility, whether he will be sedated). Do not disclose diagnosis, drug history or bloodborne-virus status for convenience.
— ask for handcuffs and any escort chain to be removed for induction, surgery and recovery.

Metal restraints are incompatible with safe positioning, venous access, diathermy return-plate placement, MRI and emergency airway access; if the security risk assessment requires them, document the discussion, the reason and who authorised it, and insist an officer with the key remains immediately available.
Comorbidity profile

— anticipate higher rates of smoking, opioid and alcohol dependence, bloodborne viruses, undertreated mental illness and self-harm; check the prison drug chart, since opioid substitution therapy (methadone or buprenorphine) must be continued and will markedly raise analgesic requirements.
Analgesia and diversion risk

— prescribe on clinical need with multimodal and regional techniques; where controlled drugs are needed, plan a supervised, non-divertible route and a clear handover plan with prison healthcare rather than under-treating pain.
Discharge and continuity

— write a discharge plan the prison healthcare team can deliver (dressings, VTE prophylaxis, analgesia, follow-up escorts), because access to review, mobilisation and simple analgesia is not guaranteed in custody.
Staff safety and dignity
— agree in advance who stays in theatre, avoid discussion of the offence, and ensure the patient is not identifiable as a prisoner to other patients any more than security requires.
Anaesthetising a handcuffed patient because nobody asked for the restraint to be removed.
Taking the history with officers at the bedside and breaching confidentiality by default.
Withholding opioid substitution therapy or adequate analgesia because of assumed drug-seeking.
Assuming the escorting officer can sign the consent form.

Provide equivalent care: he consents for himself, confidentiality is preserved as far as security allows, restraints are removed for anaesthesia unless a documented risk assessment requires otherwise, opioid substitution is continued with multimodal analgesia, and discharge is planned around what prison healthcare can deliver.

No. No adult can consent on behalf of another in England and Wales unless they hold a valid Lasting Power of Attorney for health and welfare or are a court-appointed deputy.

If the patient lacks capacity for the decision, treatment proceeds as a best-interests decision under the Mental Capacity Act 2005, consulting family and carers, and involving an IMCA where there is no one appropriate to consult.
Is it ever lawful to hold an adult still for induction of anaesthesia?

Yes, but only where the patient lacks capacity for that decision, the holding is necessary to prevent harm to them, and the degree and duration are proportionate to the likelihood and seriousness of that harm.
It should be planned in advance with named roles, documented in the best-interests record, minimised by premedication and adjustments, and reviewed afterwards.
What is a hospital passport and why does it matter to the anaesthetist?

It is a patient-held document summarising how someone with a learning disability or autism communicates, what distresses or calms them, how they show pain, their usual medication and their support needs.
It converts a chaotic day-of-surgery encounter into a planned one and should be read before the patient arrives, not after.
What should I do before reaching for sedation in a patient who cannot cooperate?

Work up the ladder: environmental and scheduling adjustments first, then preparation and desensitisation, distraction and control-giving, topical or local anaesthesia, regional techniques where suitable, and self-administered nitrous oxide/oxygen — with pharmacological premedication and inhalational induction reserved for when these are insufficient.
Document which rung succeeded so it becomes the starting point next time.

List the causes of immunosuppression encountered perioperatively and describe how they alter presentation of sepsis, wound healing and infection risk.

Outline the perioperative management of biologic and targeted synthetic therapies (anti-TNF, rituximab, tocilizumab, JAK inhibitors).
Calculate perioperative corticosteroid replacement according to surgical severity and recognise and treat adrenal crisis.
Describe the perioperative implications of HIV infection including drug interactions, organ dysfunction and post-exposure prophylaxis.
Describe the management of asplenia/hyposplenism including vaccination and lifelong antibiotic prophylaxis.

Maintenance immunosuppression (calcineurin inhibitors, antiproliferatives, corticosteroids) must never be interrupted perioperatively — use IV or NG routes if the oral route is unavailable and involve the transplant centre.

Tacrolimus and ciclosporin have a narrow therapeutic index and cause nephrotoxicity, hypertension, hyperkalaemia, hypomagnesaemia and neurotoxicity; both are CYP3A4 substrates with extensive interaction potential.

Biologics (anti-TNF, rituximab, tocilizumab) and JAK inhibitors are withheld for one full dosing interval before elective surgery and restarted once wound healing is established, to balance infection risk against disease flare.

Prednisolone ≥5 mg daily for >4 weeks suppresses the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis; perioperative hydrocortisone cover is titrated to surgical severity — minor 25–50 mg, moderate 50–100 mg then 25–50 mg 6-hourly, major 100 mg at induction then 200 mg/24 h infusion.
Ritonavir and cobicistat are potent CYP3A4 inhibitors that markedly prolong midazolam and fentanyl; efavirenz is a CYP3A4 inducer — antiretroviral therapy must not be interrupted perioperatively.

Asplenic/hyposplenic patients are at lifelong risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) with encapsulated organisms and require vaccination and lifelong penicillin V 250–500 mg twice daily.

How long before elective surgery should biologic therapies be withheld?

Typically for one full dosing interval of the specific agent (e.g. one interval for anti-TNF drugs, one infusion cycle for rituximab or tocilizumab, one dosing interval for JAK inhibitors), balancing reduced surgical site infection risk against disease flare; restart once wound healing is established.

Stop all volatile agents and suxamethonium, switch to TIVA, hyperventilate with 100% oxygen via a clean circuit, give IV dantrolene 2.5 mg/kg repeated up to 10 mg/kg (more if required), cool actively, and treat hyperkalaemia, acidosis and arrhythmias (AAGBI 2020).
Why is suxamethonium contraindicated in Duchenne and Becker muscular dystrophy?
Even sub-clinical dystrophinopathy can precipitate rhabdomyolysis and hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest after suxamethonium or prolonged volatile exposure — TIVA with non-depolarising NMBs is mandatory.
What are the airway considerations in Down syndrome?

Macroglossia, narrow nasopharynx, subglottic stenosis (use a smaller ETT than predicted) and atlanto-axial instability (careful neck positioning, neutral head) — plus a high prevalence of congenital cardiac disease and obstructive sleep apnoea.

: admit to critical care for a minimum of 24 h for monitoring of temperature, EtCO₂, potassium, CK, urine output and coagulation.
Reporting and follow-up

: report every episode to the UK Malignant Hyperthermia Registry (Leeds) and refer the patient and first-degree relatives for family screening and IVCT; document the reaction clearly and issue written information and a warning card.
Anaesthesia-induced rhabdomyolysis (AIR)
: hyperkalaemic cardiac arrest with sux ± volatiles — clinically resembles MH but is a different mechanism (membrane fragility, not RYR1).
: suxamethonium absolutely; volatiles relatively (use TIVA).
: dilated cardiomyopathy in >90% of DMD by late teens; preop echo + ECG.
: restrictive lung disease, weak cough, OSA — preop FVC, consider postop NIV.
: exaggerated response to non-depolarising NMBAs; titrate carefully with TOF; sugammadex preferred for reversal of rocuronium.
Myotonia not relieved by NMBAs, regional anaesthesia, or deep volatile — it is a sarcolemmal channelopathy. Triggers: cold, shivering, sux, neostigmine, surgical/electrical stimulation.
Treatment of intra-op contracture: local infiltration of LA into the muscle ± systemic procainamide/phenytoin/quinine.
Cardiac conduction disease (AV block) — preop ECG ± Holter; pacemaker if symptomatic. Risk of sudden death.
Bulbar weakness → aspiration risk; slow gastric emptying.
Exquisite sensitivity to opioids, benzodiazepines and propofol — use minimal doses with monitoring.
Avoid sux and neostigmine; use sugammadex.
>Managing an intra-operative myotonic crisis/contracture
Managing an intra-operative myotonic crisis/contracture

>
  • Myotonia is a sarcolemmal membrane phenomenon, not a problem at the neuromuscular junction or in central control of tone — it is therefore NOT abolished by non-depolarising neuromuscular blockade, by spinal or epidural anaesthesia, or by deepening volatile anaesthesia.

This distinguishes it clearly from malignant hyperthermia (which responds to dantrolene and removal of the trigger) and from ordinary post-operative shivering (which usually responds to warming and opioids).<InlineRef topicId=

Masseter or generalised muscle contracture can make bag-mask ventilation, laryngoscopy and surgical access impossible, even though the block appears otherwise adequate.
Direct infiltration
of the affected muscle with local anaesthetic (e.g. lidocaine) can relax a focal contracture rapidly and is often the first practical step.
Systemic membrane-stabilising drugs

: IV procainamide (where available), IV phenytoin, or quinine (historic, rarely used now) may be given for more generalised contracture. Both procainamide and phenytoin are negative inotropes and pro-arrhythmic, which is particularly hazardous in a patient who may already have underlying cardiac conduction disease.

Supportive measures: active warming and avoidance of shivering and hypothermia, minimising mechanical or electrical stimulation of muscle, and avoiding the recognised triggers — suxamethonium, neostigmine and hyperkalaemia.

>
  • Management: keep sedated and ventilated until block resolves; do NOT give neostigmine early (prolongs block); sugammadex does NOT reverse sux.
  • Send dibucaine number to confirm; family screening — autosomal recessive.
  • Acquired BChE reduction: pregnancy, liver failure, plasmapheresis, ecothiopate eye drops.

>Intraoperative and follow-up management
Intraoperative and follow-up management

>
  • Keep the patient sedated, mechanically ventilated and normothermic until neuromuscular function recovers — hypothermia and acidosis further prolong block.
  • Use quantitative (objective) neuromuscular monitoring with a peripheral nerve stimulator; do not attempt extubation until the train-of-four ratio recovers to >0.9.
  • Neostigmine is contraindicated in the early phase — it inhibits residual plasma cholinesterase activity and paradoxically prolongs the block; sugammadex has no affinity for suxamethonium (a depolarising, non-steroidal agent) and is ineffective.
  • Fresh frozen plasma or purified/recombinant BChE has been used to supply active enzyme, but its role is limited and controversial given the risks of transfusion (TRALI, infection) versus simply ventilating until natural recovery.
  • After recovery: explain the event fully to the patient and family, document clearly in the anaesthetic record and a letter to the GP, arrange an alert bracelet/card, and refer for dibucaine number/fluoride number testing and genotyping to confirm the atypical variant.
  • Offer screening to first-degree relatives — autosomal recessive inheritance means homozygous atypical individuals may show block lasting 2–8 hours, while heterozygotes typically show only mild prolongation of minutes.
