: macroglossia, midface hypoplasia, narrow nasopharynx, subglottic stenosis (use ETT 0.5–1 size smaller).
: atlanto-axial instability in 10–20% (symptomatic 1–2%). Routine X-rays not recommended; focused neuro exam — image only if symptomatic or before high-risk procedure.
: congenital heart disease affects 40–50% of individuals with Down syndrome.

Among those with CHD, the relative frequencies are approximately: atrioventricular septal defect (AVSD) ~45%, ventricular septal defect (VSD) ~35%, secundum atrial septal defect ~8%, patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) ~7%, and tetralogy of Fallot (ToF) ~4%.

Unrepaired AVSD progresses early to pulmonary hypertension and Eisenmenger physiology because of the combination of a large shunt, upper-airway obstruction and relative pulmonary hypoplasia — an up-to-date echocardiogram is needed and residual lesions/pulmonary artery pressure must be documented before non-cardiac surgery.
: OSA, hypothyroidism, leukaemia risk, recurrent chest infections, behavioural issues — premedication and parental presence often valuable.
Aorta / cardiovascular

Progressive aortic root dilatation and type-A dissection are the leading causes of death. Continue β-blockers (reduce dP/dt); target systolic BP <120 mmHg and gentle heart rate. Pre-op CT/MRI aorta if not recent. Mitral valve prolapse and regurgitation common. Place defibrillation pads if root >45 mm.
Respiratory

Pectus excavatum, kyphoscoliosis and apical bullae increase pneumothorax risk — especially with positive pressure ventilation. Use lowest airway pressures possible; high index of suspicion for spontaneous pneumothorax if desaturation or ↑airway pressures.
Ophthalmology

Lens dislocation (ectopia lentis) — upward/subluxation is characteristic. Protect eyes during positioning; avoid pressure on globes. Consider avoiding anticholinergics (less relevant in modern practice).
Neuraxial
Dural ectasia (widening of the spinal canal) makes spinal block unpredictable and increases risk of post-dural-puncture headache.

Dural ectasia also enlarges the dural sac itself, so if a dural puncture headache occurs and an epidural blood patch is required, a larger volume of autologous blood may be needed for it to be effective, the patch is technically more difficult to perform, and repeat patching is more often required.
Epidural is preferred over subarachnoid block if neuraxial technique is chosen; expect patchy spread and higher volumes needed.
Musculoskeletal

Joint laxity, scoliosis, pectus deformity and long limbs can make positioning difficult. Hyperextensible joints risk nerve stretch — pad well, avoid extreme positions. Cervical spine instability is uncommon but reported.
Practical

Continue β-blockers on day of surgery; use arterial line for beat-to-beat BP monitoring. Treat intubation response (laryngoscopy → hypertension) with opioid ± esmolol/labetalol. Avoid Valsalva, straining and hypertensive surges perioperatively.
> No association with MH. Suxamethonium and volatile agents are safe from an MH perspective, but avoid hypertensive responses to laryngoscopy and intubation.

Unlike Marfan, tortuosity and aneurysm formation are widespread throughout the arterial tree (not confined to the root), and craniofacial features — bifid or broad uvula, cleft palate, hypertelorism and craniosynostosis — help distinguish LDS clinically.

>
  • Strict blood pressure control is paramount: continue β-blockade/ARB (losartan), and blunt hypertensive surges at laryngoscopy, intubation and emergence with opioid ± esmolol/labetalol.
  • Lower the threshold for aortic imaging and surgical referral compared with Marfan given the propensity for dissection at smaller calibre vessels.
  • Generalised vascular and soft-tissue fragility affects arterial and central line placement — use ultrasound guidance and gentle technique; consider avoiding arterial cannulation unless essential.
  • Cervical spine instability has been described — take care with positioning and neck extension during airway management.
  • Caution with regional/neuraxial techniques given tissue fragility and the theoretical risk of vascular injury; dural ectasia may also occur as in Marfan.

in a closed sample (no gas exchange), cooling increases CO₂ and O₂ solubility, so their partial pressures fall, and the dissociation of buffer groups — chiefly histidine imidazole on proteins — shifts so pH rises.

alpha-stat manages ventilation using the uncorrected (37 °C) values, aiming for pH 7.40 and PaCO₂ about 5.3 kPa as measured. This keeps the ionisation state ("alpha") of histidine imidazole constant, so enzyme function and cerebral autoregulation are preserved.

A commonly taught rule of thumb is that blood pH rises by roughly 0.015 per °C of cooling; this is a textbook approximation, not a quoted figure.

water self-ionises (H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻) with ion product Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻]. Because the reaction is endothermic, Kw rises with temperature. Neutrality is defined as [H⁺] = [OH⁻], so neutral pH = ½ pKw. At 25 °C Kw ≈ 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴, giving neutral pH 7.0.

Where the equation comes from

Water ionises slightly: H₂O ⇌ H⁺ + OH⁻. The ion product, Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻], is about 10⁻¹⁴ (mol/L)² at 25 °C, so pure water has [H⁺] = [OH⁻] = 10⁻⁷ mol/L and pH 7. "Neutral" means [H⁺] equals [OH⁻] — not "pH 7".
Working out the unionised fraction
Base excess is the amount of strong acid or base required to titrate 1 L of blood back to pH 7.40 at PaCO₂ 5.3 kPa, 37 °C and full oxygenation.

For a weak acid HA ⇌ H⁺ + A⁻, Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]. Taking negative logs gives pH = pKa + log([A⁻]/[HA]). When pH equals pKa the log term is zero, so the drug is exactly 50% ionised. Each whole pH unit away from pKa changes the ratio tenfold.
Why neutral pH falls as temperature rises

For a weak base, the fraction unionised = 1 ÷ (1 + 10^(pKa − pH)). For a weak acid, it is 1 ÷ (1 + 10^(pH − pKa)). The further pH lies on the "wrong" side of pKa, the more drug is held in the charged, water-soluble form that crosses lipid membranes poorly.

Values outside ±2 mmol/L indicate a metabolic disturbance — positive in metabolic alkalosis or compensation for chronic respiratory acidosis, negative in metabolic acidosis or compensation for chronic respiratory alkalosis.

Because ionisation of water absorbs heat, warming pushes the equilibrium to the right: both [H⁺] and [OH⁻] rise together. pH falls, yet water stays neutral because the two ions are still equal. Cooling does the opposite, so neutral pH rises.

Why does CO₂ acidify blood despite not being an acid?

Always write it as pH = pKa + log([proton acceptor]/[proton donor]). For a weak acid the acceptor is the ionised A⁻; for a weak base the acceptor is the unionised B and the donor is the ionised BH⁺. This avoids having to memorise two separate formulas.

CO₂ reacts with water (carbonic anhydrase in red cells) to form H₂CO₃, which dissociates to H⁺ and HCO₃⁻. A rise in PaCO₂ pushes the equilibrium right, generating H⁺ and lowering pH — the basis of respiratory acidosis. Hyperventilation does the reverse and rapidly raises pH.

In methaemoglobin the haem iron is oxidised from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺ and cannot bind oxygen, while remaining haems bind O₂ more tightly (left-shifted curve) — so tissue delivery falls. Levels >15% cause cyanosis unresponsive to oxygen; >50% cause coma; >70% are fatal.
Redox electrochemistry
Treat with IV methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg, which regenerates Fe²⁺ via NADPH-methaemoglobin reductase.
Redox electrochemistry: labelled teaching figure showing the structures, relationships and key values FRCA and FFICM candidates need to recognise and explain for this topic.
How does a fuel cell oxygen analyser work?

A galvanic (fuel) cell consumes O₂ at a lead anode (Pb + 2OH⁻ → PbO + H₂O + 2e⁻), generating a current proportional to O₂ partial pressure at the gold cathode (O₂ + 2H₂O + 4e⁻ → 4OH⁻). It is self-powered, accurate to ±3%, and lasts typically 1–2 years because the anode is consumed.
Redox Reactions
Which inhaled anaesthetics are degraded by CO₂ absorbents?

Sevoflurane reacts with strong bases (KOH, NaOH) in soda-lime to form Compound A, a vinyl ether with renal toxicity in rats. Desflurane, enflurane and isoflurane (in descending order of risk; sevoflurane produces little) react with desiccated CO₂ absorbent to generate carbon monoxide.
Free Radicals
Both risks are mitigated by using KOH/NaOH-free absorbents (e.g. Amsorb Plus) and avoiding desiccated absorbent.
